title: More informative error in dynamic dots when LHS of `:=` is correct type but wrong size?
description:
Somewhat related to #1492, although I see that specific case will get resolved in `{glue}`.

Inside dynamic dots, if the LHS of `:=` is the correct type (string or symbol) but has size > 1, it currently errors with ``The LHS of `:=` must be a string or a symbol``:

```
library(rlang)

len1 <- "A"
len2 <- c("A", "B")

list2(!!len1 := 1)
#> $A
#> [1] 1
list2(!!len2 := 1)
#> Error in `list2()`:
#> ! The LHS of `:=` must be a string or a symbol
```

In cases where the user gets the type right but the length wrong, the intended takeaway here is the number mismatch ("**a** string or **a** symbol") but I wonder if that's too subtle and gets lost on users reading this error. Critically, I think the issue is compounded by the fact that there's no formal distinction between "string (scalar)" vs. "character (vector)" in R, so users who use "string" and "character" interchangeably might read the error as "LHS needs to be a character (vector)" which would be confusing.

Tidyverse is generally very helpful at pointing out size mismatches in error messages, and I wonder whether the error in these cases can be ``The LHS of `:=` must have size 1, not size 2``. Or if it's too complicated to do this without forcing the promise, maybe the generic error message can be augmented to emphasize the length-1 constraint a bit better, something like ``The LHS of `:=` must be a string or a symbol of size 1`` or ``The LHS of `:=` must have size 1 and be of type string or symbol``?

I feel that the error could use this extra emphasis on size because users could get stuck interpreting the error as signaling that the LHS is of incorrect type, like a function, since those cases also share the same error message (where the intended emphasis here is "a **string** or a **symbol**"):

```
list2(!!mean := 1)
#> Error in `list2()`:
#> ! The LHS of `:=` must be a string or a symbol
```

Just to add my personal experience with this: I thought `:=` could take a multi-length vector in the LHS like in data.table's `dt[, (len2) := 1]`, which doesn't work for `dplyr::mutate(df, len2 := 1)` . It took a while for me to parse the error message with emphasis on "a".

```
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
df <- tibble(x = 1:3)
new_cols <- c("y", "z")

df |> 
  mutate(!!new_cols := 0)
#> Error in `quos()`:
#> ! The LHS of `:=` must be a string or a symbol
```

Thanks!

title: Behaviour of `list2()` contradicts the docs
description:
~I'm finding a few places where~ the behaviour of `list2()` contradicts what the documentation says.

---

This comes from one of the examples.

``` r
library(rlang)

fn <- function(data, ...) {
  list2(...)
}

# Empty arguments trigger an error by default OR DO THEY?
fn(, )
#> list()
```

---

I didn't find another contradiction.

But I guess I assumed that `list2()` is like calling `dots_list()` with all of its defaults. And that is not true, which is sort of confusing, since the finer details of what `list2()` does are not documented. So the only way to learn how `dots2()` behaves with respect to names, etc. is to conduct experiments or consult the source.

``` r
library(rlang)

fn_list2 <- function(...) {
  list2(...)
}

# acts like dots_list(.named = NULL), which is not the default
fn_list2(1, 2)
#> [[1]]
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] 2
names(fn_list2(1, 2))
#> NULL

fn_dots_list <- function(...) {
  dots_list(...)
}

# we get default behaviour, which is dots_list(.named = FALSE)
fn_dots_list(1, 2)
#> [[1]]
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] 2
names(fn_dots_list(1, 2))
#> [1] "" ""
```

I think it would be helpful to say that `list2()` is like calling `dots_list()` but with a non-default choice for `.named`.

``` r
# list2(...) is equivalent to
dots_list(
  ...,
  .named = NULL # !!! not the default !!!
  # default for everything else
)
```

title: is_expression() returns FALSE on quoted function definitions
description:
From `?is_expression` :

> in rlang, an expression is the return type of parse_expr(), the set of objects that can be obtained from parsing R code

``` r
expr <- rlang::parse_expr("function(x) {x}")
rlang::is_expression(expr)
#> [1] FALSE
```

I believe the reason might be that `expr[[2]]` is a pairlist, not a symbol or call, since the doc also says : 

> is_expression() returns TRUE if the input is either a symbolic object or a syntactic literal. **If a call, the elements of the call must all be expressions as well**. Unparsable calls are not considered expressions in this narrow definition.

There might be a contradiction between these 2 quoted extracts.
I understand the appeal of the consistency of the 2nd definition (the one that is actually applied), but the 1st definition is more intuitive, maybe a `pairlist_as_language` arg and/or a note in the doc would help ?

title: `Date` and `POSIXct` are integerish
description:
I just noticed dates and times are considered integerish:
``` r
require(rlang)
#> Loading required package: rlang
d<-as.Date('2020-1-1')
is.integer(d)
#> [1] FALSE
is_integer(d)
#> [1] FALSE
is_integerish(d)
#> [1] TRUE
t<-as.POSIXct('2020-1-1 00:01:00')
is.integer(t)
#> [1] FALSE
is_integer(t)
#> [1] FALSE
is_integerish(t)
#> [1] TRUE
t<-as.POSIXct('2020-1-1 00:01:00.010')
is.integer(t)
#> [1] FALSE
is_integer(t)
#> [1] FALSE
is_integerish(t)
#> [1] FALSE
```

This makes some sense thinking about how these are stored, as they are integer like numbers internally. On the other hand boolean values fail on `is_integerish` even though they can also be presented as 0 or 1. So I'm not sure what is correct/desired. However, in the first instance, in code I was writing I expected `is_integerish` to fail on times and dates (is it maybe `is_bare_integerish` i was looking for?). I think it would be good to atleast document this behavior in `?is_integerish`  so users are aware of this.

``` r
sessionInfo(
)

title: parse_quo() doesn't use the default `env` argument
description:
Because it uses `missing()` : 

``` r
rlang::parse_quo("x")

rlang::parse_quo
#> function (x, env = global_env()) 
#> {
#>     if (missing(env)) {

#>     }
#>     new_quosure(parse_expr(x), as_environment(env))

The doc says :

title: `enexpr()` returns a quosure when provided an interpolated {{ arg }}
description:
```
library(rlang)
foo <- function(x) {
  print(enexpr(x))
  bar({{ x }})
}
bar <-function(x) {
  enexpr(x)
}

foo(y)
#> y
#> <quosure>
#> expr: ^y
#> env:  global
```

As a consequence this will have an unexpected output : 

``` r
f1 <- function(x) f2({{ x }})
f2 <- function(x) inject(aggregate(!!enexpr(x) ~ Species, iris, mean))

f2(Petal.Width)
#>      Species Petal.Width
#> 1     setosa       0.246
#> 2 versicolor       1.326
#> 3  virginica       2.026
f1(Petal.Width)
#> Error in `aggregate()`:
#> ! Base operators are not defined for quosures. Do you need to unquote
#>   the quosure?
#> 
#> # Bad: myquosure == rhs
#> 
#> # Good: !!myquosure == rhs


# workaround
f2 <- function(x) inject(aggregate(!!quo_squash(enexpr(x)) ~ Species, iris, mean))
f1(Petal.Width)
#>      Species Petal.Width
#> 1     setosa       0.246
#> 2 versicolor       1.326
#> 3  virginica       2.026
```

title: Can `as_function()` avoid materializing `call `?
description:
Right now it is materialized at every call due to `local_error_call()`

https://github.com/r-lib/rlang/blob/33db700d556b0b85a1fe78e14a53f95ac9248004/R/fn.R#L389-L393

This makes it a bit slower than it needs to be if `is_function(x)` is already true, where it could just return immediately.

An easy fix would be to put that early return for `if (is_function())` before the `local_error_call()` call, but I'm wondering if the local-error-call thing is really necessary?

title: `immediate.` option for `warn`
description:
Judging from #1397, I suspect there may be some impediment to providing this switch as available in `base::warning` but it seems like a good addition. 

A use case is when writing messages to the console for the user to keep track of where some long-running operation is at (e.g. "Processing file 2012.csv...". It makes most sense to throw a warning at the appropriate location between those log messages, so that they can take remedial action (e.g. format file "2012.csv" differently) to potentially speed up processing or facilitate computation or output in some other way.

title: should `{{ }}`work in `inject()` ? or fail elegantly ?
description:
If I understand correctly the use cases, and I might not, `inject()` is meant to be used exclusively on functions that don't support  injection/defusion.

In that case `{{ }}` is useless in those if it inlines a quosure, since these functions cannot handle those.

``` r
fun <-function(x) {
  rlang::inject({{ x }} ~ a)
}

fun(y)
#> ~y ~ a
#> <environment: 0x11a132280>
```

The above might return `y ~ a` if we make `{{ }}` equivalent to `!!enexpr()`. This would be convenient but users might miss that environments are not considered and this would be problematic in cases where it matters, e.g. if we used `data.frame({{ x }})` in `fun()` and a local `y` was defined.

Another solution might be to fail explicitly and invite the user to use `!!exexpr(x)` if they need the expression, and that they might need `eval_tidy(enquo(x))` if they want the value.

title: Consider `check_` functions
Argument `call` for `rlang::warn()` doesn't work with `dplyr::across()`
description:
Hi,

When writing helper functions, I often use the very handy `call` argument as suggested in the documentation.

This works perfectly in standard functions:

``` r
library(tidyverse)
library(rlang)

a1 = function(x){
  rlang::warn("foobar", call=caller_env())
  invisible(x)
}
a2 = function(x){
  a1(x)
}
a3 = function(){
  a2(iris$Species)
}
a3()
#> Warning message:
#> In a2(iris$Species) : foobar
```

However, it doesn't work if the function is called inside `dplyr::across()`, where the call is stuck inside:
``` r
b1 = function(){
  call = caller_env()
  iris %>% 
    mutate(across("Species", \(.x){
      rlang::warn("foobar", call=call)
      .x
    }))
  invisible()
}
b2=function() b1()
b3=function() b2()
b3()
#> Warning message:
#> Problem while computing `..1 = across(...)`.
#> i foobar
```

title: pkg_version_info comparison operator error
description:
Hi,

We have an R package whose description file is as following:

```
....
....
highcharter (== 0.8.2),
htmltools,
htmlwidgets (== 1.5.3),
httr (== 1.4.2),
...
...
```

Up to a couple of months ago, we did not have any issue while installing the package. However, in the last month or so, probably after we updated the R version, we keep getting the following error while documenting the package. 

```
Error in `check_installed()`:
! `compare` must be one of ">", ">=", "<", or "<=".
Backtrace:
    ▆
 1. └─devtools::document()
 2.   └─roxygen2::roxygenise(pkg$path, roclets)
 3.     └─roxygen2 (local) load_code(base_path)
 4.       └─pkgload::load_all(path, helpers = FALSE, attach_testthat = FALSE)
 5.         └─pkgload:::load_depends(path, quiet = quiet)
 6.           └─pkgload:::deps_check_installed(path, depends)
 7.             └─rlang::check_installed(pkg, action = action, call = call)
 8.               └─rlang:::pkg_version_info(pkg, version = version, compare = compare)
 9.                 └─rlang::abort(msg, call = call)
```

I did a bit of debugging and found out that the line which throws this error is present in the `pkg_version_info` function

```
if (!all(detect_na(info$cmp) | info$cmp %in% c(">", ">=", "<", "<="))) {
    msg <- sprintf(
      '%s must be one of ">", ">=", "<", or "<=".',
      format_arg("compare")
    )
    abort(msg, call = call)
  }
```
https://github.com/r-lib/rlang/blob/main/R/session.R#L133

Appending `==` to `info$cmp %in% c(">", ">=", "<", "<=")` seems to do the trick. However, my question is whether this is a bug or it was done on purpose?

title: Please Keep `expr_interp()` or Augment `inject()`
description:
# Context #

I recently raised [this question](https://stackoverflow.com/q/71541009) on Stack Overflow, with the following intent:

> I am developing a package, and I need a function that behaves similarly to [`rlang::inject()`](https://rlang.r-lib.org/reference/inject.html) or [`rlang::qq_show()`](https://rlang.r-lib.org/reference/qq_show.html). This function should be of the form
> 
>      unquo <- function(expr, inj_env) {
>        # ...
>      }
> which accepts an expression expr and injects the arguments from inj_env. Then it returns the injected expression itself, without evaluating it.

After some complex attempts (manipulating calls, making function factories, poking environments, etc.) to approximate this functionality, I finally stumbled across [`rlang::expr_interp()`](https://rlang.r-lib.org/reference/expr_interp.html), which is essentially _perfect_ for my needs.  It allows me to unquote a given expression in the proper context, for complex tidy evaluation.


# Issue #

Unfortunately, I notice that `expr_interp()` is deprecated in favor of `inject()`.  This loses two features:

1. The ability to obtain the unquoted expression _itself_, rather than the result of _evaluating_ it.
1. The ability to specify a separate context _from_ which various elements are injected.

Not only are these features essential to the development of my package, but they seem more broadly useful too.  The unquoted expression itself can be very useful, and users might wish to manipulate it further rather than have `inject()` execute it immediately.  Furthermore, in the spirit of the `with_*()` family, users might wish to inject a custom set of symbols, and so forth.  


# Note #

Now this behavior _could_ be approximated in messy fashion, by substituting the defused expression into `rlang::inject(base::quote(...))` and evaluating this in the injection environment.  However, this fails in an injection environment that does not inherit the ``` base::`::`() ``` function, and binding this _ad hoc_ into the environment exposes us to collisions on ``` `::` ```.


# Question #

Could `expr_interp()` please be preserved against deprecation?  Or could `inject()` be augmented with:

1. an `inj_env` parameter: the environment from which symbols (etc.) are injected?
2. an option to return the unquoted expression without evaluating it?

Below is an example of such augmentation:
```
#' For unquoting an expression object passed to the call.
unquo <- function(expr, inj_env = rlang::caller_env(), eval_env = NULL) {
  # Unquote the expression in context of injection environment.
  expr_inj <- rlang::expr_interp(expr, inj_env)
  
  # As desired: return the unquoted expression itself...
  if(rlang::is_null(eval_env)) {
    expr_inj
  }
  # ...or evaluate it in the evaluation environment.
  else {
    rlang::eval_bare(expr_inj, eval_env)
  }
}

#' For unquoting the expression captured in the call.
unquo0 <- function(expr, inj_env = rlang::caller_env(), eval_env = NULL) {
  # Capture verbatim the argument passed to 'expr'...
  expr_quo <- rlang::enquo0(expr)
  # ...and extract it literally as an expression.
  expr_lit <- rlang::quo_get_expr(expr_quo)
  
  # Unquote that expression by preference.
  unquo(expr_lit, inj_env, eval_env)
}
```

title: `srcref = TRUE` arg for `new_function()`
description:
It would be nice if `new_function()` could provide some control on the srcref, e.g. `srcref = TRUE` would be the default and keep current behaviour (consistent with `as.function()` too), `srcref = FALSE` would recursively remove the srcref related attributes.

With the current implementation I cannot easily reproduce the code to create an existing function without a srcref : 

Here's an attempt to recreate `stats::ave()`

``` r
args_ <- alist(x =, ... =, FUN = mean)
body_ <- quote({
  if (missing(...)) 
    x[] <- FUN(x)
  else {
    g <- interaction(...)
    split(x, g) <- lapply(split(x, g), FUN)
  }
  x
})
env_ <- asNamespace("stats")

waldo::compare(
  rlang::new_function(args_, body_, env_),
  ave,
  ignore_srcref = FALSE
)
#> `attr(body(old), 'srcfile')` is an S3 object of class <srcfilecopy/srcfile>, an environment
#> `attr(body(new), 'srcfile')` is absent
#> 
#> `attr(body(old), 'srcref')` is a list
#> `attr(body(new), 'srcref')` is absent
#> 
#> `attr(body(old), 'wholeSrcref')` is an S3 object of class <srcref>, an integer vector
#> `attr(body(new), 'wholeSrcref')` is absent
#> 
#> `attr(body(old)[[2]][[4]], 'srcfile')` is an S3 object of class <srcfilecopy/srcfile>, an environment
#> `attr(body(new)[[2]][[4]], 'srcfile')` is absent
#> 
#> `attr(body(old)[[2]][[4]], 'srcref')` is a list
#> `attr(body(new)[[2]][[4]], 'srcref')` is absent
#> 
#> `attr(body(old)[[2]][[4]], 'wholeSrcref')` is an S3 object of class <srcref>, an integer vector
#> `attr(body(new)[[2]][[4]], 'wholeSrcref')` is absent
```

<sup>Created on 2022-07-04 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.1)</sup>


Note that  `identical(rlang::new_function(args_, body_, env_), ave)` is `FALSE`, I believe the default `ignore.srcref = TRUE` probably applies only on the outer layer.

title: Find the OO system used for an object
`call` arg ignored for `.internal = TRUE` in `cli_abort()`
description:
`cli::cli_abort(.internal = TRUE)` internal error messages always assume the error would be **in the cli package**, regardless of `call`. `rlang::abort(.internal = TRUE)` doesn't have this problem.

``` r
good <- function() rlang::abort("oops", call = rlang::caller_env(), .internal = TRUE)
bad <- function() cli::cli_abort("oops", call = rlang::caller_env(), .internal = TRUE)

good()
#> Error:
#> ! oops
#> ℹ This is an internal error, please report it to the package authors.
bad()
#> Error:
#> ! oops
#> ℹ This is an internal error in the cli package, please report it to the package
#>   authors.
```

<sup>Created on 2022-03-31 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.1)</sup>

I think the underlying issue is in `rlang::abort()`:

https://github.com/r-lib/rlang/blob/9d8e74f1d09622028e1be6268153a930ad6ea333/R/cnd-abort.R#L300-L307 uses `cnd_message_info(call = caller)` but instead should be `cnd_message_info(call = call)` because [`caller <- caller_env()`](https://github.com/r-lib/rlang/blob/9d8e74f1d09622028e1be6268153a930ad6ea333/R/cnd-abort.R#L253).

title: could trace_back() better annotate functions "hidden" in closures?
description:
For example, consider the following:

```
library(rlang)
trace(getOption, quote(print(rlang::trace_back())))
local({ rlang:::defer(42) })
```

I see:

```
Tracing getOption("knitr.in.progress") on entry 
     ▆
  1. ├─base::local(...)
  2. │ └─base::eval.parent(substitute(eval(quote(expr), envir)))
  3. │   └─base::eval(expr, p)
  4. │     └─base::eval(expr, p)
  5. └─base::eval(...)
  6.   └─base::eval(...)
  7.     └─rlang:::defer(42)
  8.       └─rlang add_handler(...)
  9.         └─rlang exit_frame(envir, frames, calls)
 10.           └─rlang in_knitr(envir)
 11.             └─rlang knitr_in_progress()
 12.               ├─base::isTRUE(getOption("knitr.in.progress"))
 13.               └─base::getOption("knitr.in.progress")
```

The "internal" functions like `in_knitr` and `knitr_in_progress` are marked as part of the `rlang` namespace, but IMHO it could be made more explicit that those are part of a separate internal closure somehow.

For what it's worth, this was prompted by me reading that output and thinking I would've been able to reference those functions via `rlang:::in_knitr`, but that failed since they're really in `defer()`, e.g. you could find them in `environment(rlang:::defer)$in_knitr`)

(feel free to close if you feel this is too narrow, since this pattern shouldn't be especially common)

title: Confusing error message in `as_version_info()`
description:
Related to [this issue](https://github.com/r-lib/roxygen2/issues/1275) I raised for roxygen2:

The problem, having a malformed (name, version) tuple in an item in for example `Depends:` or `Imports` is handled better when using the very latest versions of `pkgload` and `rlang`. The improved error message shows:

```R
Error in `check_installed()`:
! Can't parse version in `pkg`.
Run `rlang::last_error()` to see where the error occurred.
```

I think this message is a tiny bit confusing as the user doesn't have `pkg` anywhere in their code. However, this error is `as_version_info()` which has as argument the individual items. I think it would be more helpful to show the first offending item (or maybe all items).

title: Any interest in `capture_args()`?
description:
In keras, I've implemented a pure-R version of a helper function named [`capture_args()`](https://github.com/rstudio/keras/blob/6debf31b9a6e52a4ef4f0583a618a7a922c4b2c6/R/utils.R#L413). It's intent is to capture the values of what the user called a function with, as if they had written `base::list(...)` instead of `<keras_fn>(...)`.

This is useful because it lets the keras R package easily maintain compatibility with older versions of tensorflow, while still presenting only the latest function signatures in the R wrappers.

Due to some peculiarities of how it's implemented, it has some inconvenient restrictions such as, `match.call()` must be part of the call, `capture_args()` itself can't be evaluated in another call (e.g., `do.call(fn, capture_args()` fails), it potentially reorders arguments that matched to `...` in the originating call, and, it can't handle positional-only unnamed args in `...`. These deficiencies would probably best be resolved by re-writing it in C, but we currently don't have any compiled code in the keras package and I'd rather keep keras pure R if possible. Keras already has an rlang dependency however. Would there be any interest in adding a better, implemented-in-C `capture_args()` to rlang? (or maybe there is something that already does this in rlang that I overlooked?)

title: Feedback tidy eval documentation
description:
Specifically on [Data mask programming patterns](https://rlang.r-lib.org/reference/topic-data-mask-programming.html#transforming-inputs-with-across-) (#1307 ).

## Move Argument Behaviors

Consider moving "Argument behaviours" section to a separate vignette or somewhere else within the "Data Mask Programming Behaviors". I felt like "Choosing a Pattern" sets-up the Forwarding, Name, Bridge patterns and I would have rather just gotten into the examples (i.e. start the "Forwarding" section) rather than having the "Argument behaviors" section come in between them. Or maybe just shorten it in some way... I did like it's description on how to document these in your own functions, I just found it's location (as well as how abstract the section is compared to the more concrete, example filled sections that follow it) added some cognitive load for me while going through the vignette.

## Add Transformation Patterns to "Choosing a Pattern" section

You set-up Forwarding, Name, and Bridge Patterns, here:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/30487784/142704100-bcb10795-12e8-46ae-b2ec-091e01c83864.png)

but don't mention **Transformation Patterns** a wording you use at the end of the vignette.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/30487784/142704329-c43dd06e-b502-4e53-b4af-6e4e82146958.png)


## Clarify meaning of "template"

For this section:

>For inputs in ... however, this technique does not work. We would need some kind of templating syntax for dots that lets us specify R code with a placeholder for the dots elements. This isn't built in tidy eval but you can use operators like dplyr::across(), dplyr::if_all(), or dplyr::if_any(). When that isn't possible, you can template the expression manually.

Maybe adjust wording or add a hyperlink to an example on what "templating syntax" or "template" means in this context...

## Typo

> The easiest way it to forward the dots

See typo, "it" should be "is"

If this isn't supported, are you open to adding a utility for it? Something like the following (as a concept):

as.list.rlang_data_pronoun <- function(x, ...) {
  mask <- .subset2(x, 1)

  Reduce(
    function(env, lst) utils::modifyList(lst, as.list(env)),

    init = list(),

  )
}

title: Question: how to evaluate expressions that can be evaluated and leave unevaluated those that can't?
description:
Is it possible to automatically evaluate those defused expressions that contain symbols that can be resolved, and leave as defused those that can't?

Here's an example of what I am trying to achieve:

```R
library(rlang)
  
`%/.%` <- substitute
{x + x^2 + a + b} %/.% exprs(x = 3)
```

which returns:

```R
{
    3 + 3^2 + a + b
}
```

I would like a way to make it return `12 + a +  b`, so resolving the `x` to `3` and `x^2` to `3^2`, and then to `9`, and finally add `3 + 9`, i.e. `12`, but leave `a` and `b` unevaluated because they can't be looked up in the current environment.

Is this possible?

I am drawing inspiration from the first example from Mathematica documentation here: https://reference.wolfram.com/language/ref/Rule.html.

BTW: I couldn't run reprex on this example: https://github.com/tidyverse/reprex/issues/412.

The motivation for my question is really just to learn NSE with `{rlang}` at this point.

EDIT: Now that I am thinking, I am guessing this is not possible... The notion of what can and can't be evaluated cannot be determined without actually attempting to evaluate the expressions, right?

title: Function-style syntax for {{
description:
Please consider adding a function-style alternative syntax for `{{`.  I suggest using the name `forward_arg`.  User code would then look like:
```
my_mean <- function(data, var) {
  dplyr::summarise(data, mean = mean(forward_arg(var)))
}
```

 The advantages of doing so would be:
- easier to read and understand, particularly for people not familiar with `{{`
- easier to search for in documentation and web search

It also makes it possible to define a function you can both document and that gives a helpful error message if `forward_arg` is used in an incorrect context.
```
#' <documentation of the way forward_arg works in a tidyeval context>
forward_arg <- function(arg) {
  stop("forward_arg() only supported in tidyeval contexts.")
}
```

title: print names of .onLoad functions in traceback?
description:
For example:

```
> trace(dyn.load, quote(print(rlang::trace_back())))
Tracing function "dyn.load" in package "base"
[1] "dyn.load"
> library(RcppParallel)
Tracing dyn.load(path, local = FALSE, now = TRUE) on entry 
     ▆
  1. └─base::library(RcppParallel)
  2.   ├─base::tryCatch(...)
  3.   │ └─base tryCatchList(expr, classes, parentenv, handlers)
  4.   │   └─base tryCatchOne(expr, names, parentenv, handlers[[1L]])
  5.   │     └─base doTryCatch(return(expr), name, parentenv, handler)
  6.   └─base::loadNamespace(package, lib.loc)
  7.     └─base runHook(".onLoad", env, package.lib, package)
  8.       ├─base::tryCatch(fun(libname, pkgname), error = identity)
  9.       │ └─base tryCatchList(expr, classes, parentenv, handlers)
 10.       │   └─base tryCatchOne(expr, names, parentenv, handlers[[1L]])
 11.       │     └─base doTryCatch(return(expr), name, parentenv, handler)
 12.       └─RcppParallel fun(libname, pkgname)
 13.         └─RcppParallel:::loadTbbLibrary("tbb")
 14.           └─base::dyn.load(path, local = FALSE, now = TRUE)
 ```

Note that the traceback reports RcppParallel's `.onLoad()` function as `RcppParallel fun(libname, pkgname)`. I would've expected to see `RcppParallel:::.onLoad(libname, pkgname)` instead.

My best guess is that this happens because the function is assigned to a variable `fun` and called here, when loaded via `loadNamespace()`:

https://github.com/wch/r-source/blob/d3c735e8b5d4a4ac527958b24ede3699fcd0f4b3/src/library/base/R/namespace.R#L241-L244

This issue is pretty minor since the traceback already makes it clear from `runHook(".onLoad", ...)` that we'll be running the `.onLoad()` hook, though.

title: Consider making `as_label()` generic
description:
`as_label()` is an extremely useful function for generating a concise, single-line text representation of an arbitrary object. Sometimes I do find myself wanting more customizability however. It currently dispatches to `pillar::type_sum()` which does not work well for all cases, as it can be useful for a generated label to be different from the column summary label.

Proposed change:  make `as_label()` generic and move the current implementation to `as_label.default()`

title: Deparsing API
description:
#### `expr_deparse()`

Currently its behaviour is not well defined. I think it should be designed in terms of roundtrip and fallback modes.

Roundtrip modes:

- Parse (default): Non-reparsable inputs (injected objects) are not deparsed. If this mode is selected and if the fallback is not set, an input is guaranteed to be recreated exactly by `base::parse()` or fail with an error.

- Parse-Eval: Inlined and structured objects are deparsed with calls to `c()`, `structure()`, etc. In this mode, an input is guaranteed to be recreated exactly by a combination of `base::parse()` + `base::eval(envir = baseenv())`. This mode is partly similar to the behaviour of `base::deparse()` but not completely (base parse and deparse do not roundtrip exactly in the presence of inlined objects).
  
A `roundtrip` argument to choose between `"parse"` and `"parse-eval"` would be low priority to implement (perhaps never). However it's useful to frame the behaviour `expr_deparse()` in terms of a parse-deparse roundtrip.

Fallback: `NULL` or a custom function.

- Error: This ensures non-reparsable (or non-reparse-evalable) objects cause an error.
- Custom: Can be a function like `as_label()` that transforms the object into a string.

Printing inlined vectors:

Currently `expr_print()`, used in the quosure print method, prints inlined vectors as: `<chr: "foo", "bar", ...>`. This would have to be handled by a fallback function, such as `vec_format()`:

```r
expr_deparse(
  roundtrip = "parse",
  fallback = vec_format
)
```

If rlang had its own parsing function where the `<vec: ...>` syntax defines a vector literal, this could be folded in a roundtrip mode (not planned).


#### `as_label()`

`as_label()` describes an expression in a short string that doesn't contain any newline. It is used for:

- Automatically labelling new columns created from unnamed expressions in tidyeval APIs.
- Summarising user input in error messages.

The goal is to describe an object, not to represent it.

- Quosures are squashed
- Function calls are deparsed
- Evaluated formulas are deparsed without attributes
- Vectors of size > 1 and structured objects are formatted with `pillar::type_sum()`

Future:

- Currently doesn't use `expr_deparse()`, but it probably should. Can we afford the behaviour change and the performance hit?
- A `width` argument would be nice.
- The call part should be factored out as a `call_deparse_line()` function. Would be used for things like backtraces.

title: Should trace API interact with `.__error_call__.`?
description:
`rlang`recently added an extremely useful feature of overriding the error call in a local environment (in form of `.__error_call__.` and `local_error_call()`). This is great for auxiliary checking functions that have to perform checks on behalf of other functions for example. 

I was wondering whether it would be a good idea if `trace_back()` inferred `bottom` from `.__error_call__ .` in case the latter is an environment. This could potentially produce cleaner traces that omit the auxiliary functions entirely. E.g.

```r
library(rlang)

check <- function(x) {
  .__error_call__. <- caller_env()
  (x>0) || abort("must be positive")
}

f <- function(x) {
  check(x)
  x*2
}

f(-1)
```

currently produces 

```
Error in `f()`: must be positive
Backtrace:
    ▆
 1. └─global f(-1)
 2.   └─global check(x)
```

If trace would use the information in `  .__error_call__.`, the error produced instead would state:

```
Error in `f()`: must be positive
Backtrace:
    ▆
 1. └─global f(-1)
```

title: Deprecate `with_env()` and `locally()`
description:
`with_env` allows us to evaluate expressions in an environment, including setting values in the environment:

```r
e <- new.env()

rlang::with_env(e, {
  x <- 1
  y <- 2
  f <- function(x) print(x)
  g <- function() f(1)
})

e$x
#> [1] 1
e$g()
#> [1] 1
```

However, it doesn't support quasiquotation, which means we can't trivially write a function which takes an expression and evaluates it in an environment.

``` r
set_in_env <- function(expr) {
  e <- new.env()
  
  q <- rlang::enquo(expr)
  
  rlang::with_env(e, !!q)
  rlang::with_env(e, {x <- 1})
  
  return(e)
}

e <- set_in_env({y <- 2})
#> Error: Quosures can only be unquoted within a quasiquotation context. [...]
```

<sup>Created on 2021-10-26 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.1)</sup>

As mentioned by [@MrFlick on SO][1], we can use `inject` to build the call:

```r
set_in_env <- function(expr) {  
  e <- new.env()

  q <- rlang::enexpr(expr)

  rlang::inject(rlang::with_env(e, !!q))
  rlang::with_env(e, {x <- 1})
  
  return(e)
}
```

This works, but it feels like a workaround and not like the most proper and idiomatic way of doing it. Would allowing unquotation in `with_env` be possible or is there a reason for this that hasn't occurred to me?

[1]: https://stackoverflow.com/a/69729311/2175231

title: Aggressive ellipsizing in as_label
description:
#1277 changed the behavior of `as_label` when the call contains operators. On current release of rlang, we see:

```
> as_label(quote(nchar(chr, type = "bytes", allowNA = TRUE) == 1))
[1] "nchar(chr, type = \"bytes\", allowNA = TRUE) == 1"
```

On dev rlang, we get

```
> as_label(quote(nchar(chr, type = "bytes", allowNA = TRUE) == 1))
[1] "... == 1"
```

The [tests](https://github.com/r-lib/rlang/commit/4ee1b05869272ad76c0a5247427549a78ac06775#diff-37deb3c3c1079c1f5433d780f478e3e2c9a8fae1fe70fcf3e02cb5c85d856514R618-R623) added in #1277 show that this is intentional behavior, but I wonder if this is too aggressive in shortening the output. Judging from the [criteria](https://github.com/r-lib/rlang/commit/4ee1b05869272ad76c0a5247427549a78ac06775#diff-9bea1e8787a8eaa532a36952bbdb166d6bee31fcdb8e00063abc8a09546f8445R899-R900) for whether to insert `...`, it looks like it is trying to hold to `deparse`'s default 60-character width (28 + 29 + 3 for the operator). But we aren't exceeding that in the example above, it's just that the left side is longer than 28 chars:

```
> nchar("nchar(chr, type = \"bytes\", allowNA = TRUE) == 1")
[1] 47
```

I understand the use case that #1277 intended to fix, but I'm wondering if you'd be interested in a PR that would limit this new behavior to where the total width of the deparsed expression was greater than 60 characters?

title: Supersede `ensym()` in favour of `enstring()` or `check_ensym()`
description:
It is sometimes needed to take column names instead of flexible expressions in functions that interface with data-masked verbs.

- Restricting the inputs to existing column names is an easy way of avoiding problems of double evaluations.

- Column names are also easier to work with when creating a default result name in the output. You can paste a prefix or suffix to the input name without wondering what happens with complex expressions.

- In some cases, creating a new vector on the fly complicates things. Maybe two separate computations are performed on the same column name, and it's not always obvious to users that `{{` in action verbs allows creating new vectors when a complex expression is passed.

In general, taking simple columns makes things easier. Currently the way to do this is `ensym()` which returns a symbol. There are two alternatives that could improve things.

#### `enstring()`

1. Unlike `ensym()`, `enstring()` would not accept quoted strings as input. This flexibility is inherited from early tidyr interfaces but causes confusion. It suggests the function accepts regular strings instead of data-masked arguments.

2. It would return a string, an object easier to work with than symbols.

3.  Although `.data[[foo]]` supports symbols, it would be more obvious that the result of `enstring()` can be used to subset `.data`. Users would have to go out of their way (transform to symbol) to inject the string instead of subsetting `.data`.

Compare:

```r
function(data, var) {
  summarise(data, mean(.data[[enstring(var)]]))
}

function(data, var) {
  summarise(data, mean(!!sym(enstring(var))))
}
```

Subsetting `.data` should always be preferred because unquoting a naked symbol is not hygienic. If the variable doesn't exist in the data frame, R will look up the chain of environments, starting from the current env since the symbol is not quosured.

#### `check_ensym()`

Alternatively, we could check that a defused argument is a symbol, and then use `{{`. I think this would be my preferred solution:

```r
function(data, var) {
  check_ensym(var)
  summarise(data, mean({{ var }}))
}
```

However `check_ensym()` has a downside. Unlike subsetting `.data`, it doesn't ensure that the column name exists. When it doesn't exist, R will look up the environment hierarchy for a variable with the same name. We are using `{{` here so we do track the original environment. This is more hygienic than an unquoted symbol where the tracked environment is the current env instead of the caller env. However, it seems that in most cases, finding a variable in the user environment would be a bug.

Maybe we could make `data` an argument:

```r
function(data, var) {
  check_ensym(data, var)
  summarise(data, mean({{ var }}))
}
```

You could supply `NULL` to allow any names.

It seems like this pattern would offer a better separation in programming patterns:

- Subset the `.data` pronoun when you take a regular string.
- Use `{{` when you take a data-masked expression. Add `check_ensym()` to restrict it to a symbol.

cc @hadley


Note: In both cases, users would still be able to supply `.data[[foo]]` expressions. This way a function that uses `check_ensym()` or `enstring()` can still be easily used in `map()` or `for` loops by subsetting `.data` at the call site.

library(rlang)

title: Ensure all dots are named/unnamed in `dots_list()`
description:
It would be nice to have an option to ensure that all dots are named (or unnamed). Currently `dots_list()` only has an auto-naming option with `.named = TRUE`. To ensure all dots are named, a small workaround like this is required: 

```
library(rlang)
dots_list_named <- function(...){
  dots <- dots_list(..., .named = FALSE)
  if(! is_named(dots))
    abort("")
  dots
}
dots_list(x = 1, 2)
dots_list_named(x = 1, 2)
```

Ideally, this would be included in the `.named` argument, but this changes the function's current behavior.
```
.named = c("default", "build", "all", "none")
``` 
More practical would be to include an `.ensure_named` argument taking values, but this might conflict with the `.named = TRUE` behavior.
```
.ensure_named = c("false", "named",  "unnamed")
```

title: Empty quosures can not be turned into callable functions
description:

``` r

fn()
#> Error in fn(): object '' not found
```

<sup>Created on 2021-07-23 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.0)</sup>

I'm expecting the body of the function to not throw an error, such as `function(){}` to be returned from `rlang::as_function(quo())`.

I have a workaround using `quo_is_missing()`.

```r

title: Build system prepends DESTDIR on mkdir calls during the make phase
description:
First noticed here https://github.com/kisslinux/kiss/issues/258

The build system assumes that `DESTDIR` is only set during the `install` phase (which is an incorrect assumption to make).
This behaviour is unexpected, the result of this is that it prepends `DESTDIR` to the `mkdir` calls that lead to breaking builds.

A workaround for this is by adding `DESTDIR=""` in the make phase.

title: Stateful iterator of object trees
description:
Context: https://rpubs.com/wch/735368

Goals:

* Performance (no intermediary data structures, no recursion)
* Avoid stack overflow
* Provide a structured and straightforward template for traversal tasks

UI-wise, the user should be in control of how to traverse the nodes of the tree. This implies a stateful iterator with a `push()` method to which new nodes are supplied. The nodes would be traversed in depth-first order (at least by default).

The most flexible UI for consumption of the tree elements is pull-based (see https://greim.github.io/gen/dist/01-pull-push.html). This could be achieved by taking an `enum()` function of two arguments.

- The first argument is the iterator state. It has a `push()` method for adding nodes onto the stack of objects to visit in depth-first order.

- The second argument is the object being visited. If this is a node you can optionally push all or some of its children nodes onto the stack via the first argument.

`enum()` determines which objects are traversed via the `push()` method. It also determines which objects are visited by the iterator: any object returned by `enum()` becomes an iterator element. Return `NULL` to skip.

```r
find_symbols <- function(x) {
  enum <- function(it, x) {
    switch(typeof(x),
      # Visit symbols
      symbol = x,
      # Traverse calls, environments, and functions
      language = it$push(!!!x),
      environment = it$push(!!!as.list(x)),
      closure = it$push(body(x), formals(x)),
      NULL
    )
  }
  it <- new_sexp_iterator(x, enum)

  syms <- env()

  # If the iterator is implemented using the coro protocol
  coro::loop(for (elt in it) {
    # Collect symbols in a hash table
    env_poke(syms, elt, TRUE)
  })

  env_names(syms)
}
```

(We might want to reconsider a rich value for iterator exhaustion in coro instead of a sentinel value because the above will be buggy if the namespace contains the sentinel, which it very well could - This is something @gaborcsardi warned me about many times but I thought traversing language objects would be very rare).

The alternative is a push-based UI. It is less flexible but as @gaborcsardi mentioned on Slack it may be considerably faster in some cases because the looping is purely C-based.

```r
find_symbols <- function(x) {
  syms <- env()

  # In this case the return value of `enum()` is ignored
  enum <- function(it, x) {
    switch(typeof(x),
      symbol = env_poke(syms, x, TRUE),
      language = it$push(!!!x),
      environment = it$push(!!!as.list(x)),
      closure = it$push(body(x), formals(x)),
      NULL
    )
  }

  tree_map(x, enum)
  env_names(syms)
}
```

title: More robust data mask rechaining
description:
Currently the lexical scope of environments that escape data masking contexts is rather undefined. These environments consistently include the masked data but beyond that it depends which quosure was first evaluated:

```r
e1 <- NULL
q1 <- local({
  foo <- 10
  e1 <<- environment()
  quo(environment())
})

e2 <- NULL
q2 <- local({
  foo <- "wrong"
  e2 <<- environment()
  quo(identity(!!q1))
})

out <- eval_tidy(q2)

evalq(foo, out)
#> [1] "wrong"

identical(env_parent(out), e2)
#> [1] TRUE
```

That's because of the way data masks are rechained to the quosure env as evaluation progresses from one quosure to the next.

This strategy causes pain for some metaprogramming tasks such as quosure expansion in `dplyr::across()` (cc @romainfrancois), making it difficult to create quosures inside data masks. We are now at our third patch release of dplyr to deal with edge cases related to this.

An alternative rechaining strategy that would be more predictable and easier to work with would be as follows:

- Create a new execution environment before evaluating each quosure.
- Set the parent of that exec env to the data mask. Set the data mask top to the quosure env.
- After evaluation, set the parent of the exec env back to the quosure env. Set the data mask top to the empty env.

With this design all environments created within data masks would consistently inherit from their original lexical environment. On the other hand, they would no longer inherit from the data mask, which is a potentially important breaking change. We would need to assess damage for tidyverse and tidymodels reverse dependencies (cc @topepo @DavisVaughan).

Unquoting language objects with `!!!` is deprecated as of rlang 0.4.0.

data("starwars")
foo <- function(x, ...) {
  temp <- enquos(...)
  group_by(x, !!!temp[[1]]) %>% tally()
}
foo(starwars, sex, gender) # Will ignore gender in this case
```

What would be the correct way of doing this? Thanks!

title: object 'testthat_print' not found
description:
```lang-r
devtools::document(...) # some local package
# Error in get(genname, envir = envir) : object 'testthat_print' not found
```

There is no code change required for this issue, just awareness of the source of the problem and its fix. Whether you blog it or tweet it or just keep this issue open and pinned for a while is up to you.

## The Fix

Update `testthat` to 3.0.0 or newer.

If you haven't upgraded to `rlang-0.4.10` yet, when you do, make sure you include `"Suggests"` in the `dependencies=` argument, as in

```lang-r
install.packages("rlang", dependencies = c("Depends", "Imports", "LinkingTo", "Suggests"))
```

(That includes 14 packages, it's possible one or more will be new to you.)

## Background

Stemming from https://github.com/r-lib/devtools/issues/2309, the issue arises because `rlang` can be updated while ignoring some of its dependencies.

Specifically, `testthat::testthat_print` was added (https://github.com/r-lib/testthat/commit/07b19c87e2a3465ceb155570bd86ae68c75a2350) before testthat3 was released. `rlang` started using it around the same time (https://github.com/r-lib/rlang/commit/bfb1d4130a811a99ca190cc88077eab08ea2a5d8), before it released rlang-0.4.10. So far, so good.

Unfortunately, `testthat` is in rlang's `Suggests:`, and the default for `install.packages` is `dependencies=NA` which only considers `c("Depends", "Imports", "LinkingTo")`.

title: `cnd_message()` is called twice in `rlang::abort()` within `reprex::reprex()`
description:
Disclaimer: I do understand this is an experimental feature, but to me this looks like an exceptionally important feature for package maintainers and users of {rlang}.

`rlang::abort()` allows throwing errors of a derived type with additional data attached to them. This is great for extensibility, as consumers of {rlang} can define their own error class and provide some generics to improve error printing. At the same time, consumers can rely on {ralng}'s formatting methods for `rlang_error`, which print out additional info like backtraces, parents, etc.

Right now, the suggested approach is to [implement `S3` generics](https://rlang.r-lib.org/reference/cnd_message.html) `rlang::cnd_header()`, `rlang::cnd_body()`, `rlang::cnd_footer()` for a derived type to improve printing. 
The default implementation used for formatting `ralgn_error` seems to just return the `$message` field in `cnd_header.default()`.
So, if one would like to print additional info (e.g., using metadata attached as fields to the thrown error), all the logic can be put in, say, `cnd_header()`. 

At this point, I assume that `S3` can be used to implement a proper 'virtual' method using something like
```r
cnd_header.my_error <- function(cnd, ...) paste(NextMethod(), custom_message(cnd), sep = "\n")
```
The expected behavior is that when printed, `my_error` will display both its `$message` field through default implementation and some additional info.

Here is a reprex with inheritance. I copy-paste the output:
<details>
<summary>Code</summary>

```r
cnd_header.a <- function(cnd, ...)  paste(NextMethod(), "A", sep = "\n")
cnd_header.b <- function(cnd, ...)  paste(NextMethod(), "B", sep = "\n")
err <- tryCatch(rlang::abort("Original message", c("b", "a")), error = identity)
print(err)
summary(err)
```
</details>

<details>
<summary>Regular output</summary>

```
<error/b>
Original message
A
B
Backtrace:
 1. base::source(...)
 5. base::tryCatch(...)
 6. base:::tryCatchList(expr, classes, parentenv, handlers)
 7. base:::tryCatchOne(expr, names, parentenv, handlers[[1L]])
 8. base:::doTryCatch(return(expr), name, parentenv, handler)
<error/b>
Original message
A
B
Backtrace:
    x
 1. +-base::source(...)
 2. | +-base::withVisible(eval(ei, envir))
 3. | \-base::eval(ei, envir)
 4. |   \-base::eval(ei, envir)
 5. \-base::tryCatch(...)
 6.   \-base:::tryCatchList(expr, classes, parentenv, handlers)
 7.     \-base:::tryCatchOne(expr, names, parentenv, handlers[[1L]])
 8.       \-base:::doTryCatch(return(expr), name, parentenv, handler)
```
</details>

However, this is what happens if instead this same snippet is executed using {reprex}:
<details>
<summary>Reprex</summary>

```r
cnd_header.a <- function(cnd, ...)  paste(NextMethod(), "A", sep = "\n")
cnd_header.b <- function(cnd, ...)  paste(NextMethod(), "B", sep = "\n")
err <- tryCatch(rlang::abort("Original message", c("b", "a")), error = identity)
print(err)
#> <error/b>
#> Original message
#> A
#> B
#> A
#> B
#> Backtrace:
#>  1. base::tryCatch(...)
#>  2. base:::tryCatchList(expr, classes, parentenv, handlers)
#>  3. base:::tryCatchOne(expr, names, parentenv, handlers[[1L]])
#>  4. base:::doTryCatch(return(expr), name, parentenv, handler)
summary(err)
#> <error/b>
#> Original message
#> A
#> B
#> A
#> B
#> Backtrace:
#>     x
#>  1. \-base::tryCatch(...)
#>  2.   \-base:::tryCatchList(expr, classes, parentenv, handlers)
#>  3.     \-base:::tryCatchOne(expr, names, parentenv, handlers[[1L]])
#>  4.       \-base:::doTryCatch(return(expr), name, parentenv, handler)
```

<sup>Created on 2021-05-14 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.0)</sup>

</details>

The messages written by derived methods actually repeat themselves twice. I spent a lot of time trying to understand what is going on. The problem can be understood if a traceback is printed from the derived formatting method:

<details>
<summary>With traces </summary>

``` r
cnd_header.with_trace <- function(cnd, ...) {
  print("Printing trace:")
  print(rlang::trace_back())
  paste(NextMethod(), "with_trace", sep = "\n")
}
rlang::abort("rlang", "with_trace")
#> [1] "Printing trace:"
#>      x
#>   1. \-rlang::abort("rlang", "with_trace")
#>   2.   \-rlang:::signal_abort(cnd)
#>   3.     +-base::conditionMessage(cnd)
#>   4.     \-rlang:::conditionMessage.rlang_error(cnd)
#>   5.       \-rlang::cnd_message(c)
#>   6.         +-rlang:::paste_line(cnd_header(cnd), cnd_body(cnd), cnd_footer(cnd))
#>   7.         | \-rlang::chr(...)
#>   8.         |   \-rlang::dots_values(...)
#>   9.         +-rlang::cnd_header(cnd)
#>  10.         \-global::cnd_header.with_trace(cnd)
#> [1] "Printing trace:"
#>      x
#>   1. \-rlang::abort("rlang", "with_trace")
#>   2.   \-rlang:::signal_abort(cnd)
#>   3.     \-base::stop(fallback)
#>   4.       +-base::conditionMessage(cond)
#>   5.       \-rlang:::conditionMessage.rlang_error(cond)
#>   6.         \-rlang::cnd_message(c)
#>   7.           +-rlang:::paste_line(cnd_header(cnd), cnd_body(cnd), cnd_footer(cnd))
#>   8.           | \-rlang::chr(...)
#>   9.           |   \-rlang::dots_values(...)
#>  10.           +-rlang::cnd_header(cnd)
#>  11.           \-global::cnd_header.with_trace(cnd)
#> Error: rlang
#> with_trace
#> with_trace
#> [1] "Printing trace:"
#>      x
#>   1. +-base::tryCatch(...)
#>   2. | \-base:::tryCatchList(expr, classes, parentenv, handlers)
#>   3. |   +-base:::tryCatchOne(...)
#>   4. |   | \-base:::doTryCatch(return(expr), name, parentenv, handler)
#>   5. |   \-base:::tryCatchList(expr, names[-nh], parentenv, handlers[-nh])
#>   6. |     \-base:::tryCatchOne(expr, names, parentenv, handlers[[1L]])
#>   7. |       \-base:::doTryCatch(return(expr), name, parentenv, handler)
#>   8. +-base::withCallingHandlers(...)
#>   9. +-base::saveRDS(...)
#>  10. +-base::do.call(...)
#>  11. +-(function (what, args, quote = FALSE, envir = parent.frame()) ...
#>  12. \-(function (input) ...

For some reason, when executed with {reprex}, the `cnd_message()` gets called twice, and its results are accumulated.
This is likely the place the first time `cnd_message()` is called via `conditionMessage.rlang_error()`.
https://github.com/r-lib/rlang/blob/bda055d61dd67a57da64e066be8501ba6d750824/R/cnd-abort.R#L198-L210
The message gets formatted and written to the `$message` field of `fallback`.
And then the second trace originates from here:
https://github.com/r-lib/rlang/blob/bda055d61dd67a57da64e066be8501ba6d750824/R/cnd-abort.R#L220-L222
Where `cnd_message()` gets called on an **already modified** `fallback`, so the message is duplicated. And this behavior somehow depends on how it's being executed.

This seems to occur in `rlang::abort()` and `rlang:::signal_abort()` (perhaps in the base `signalCondition()`). 
If an error condition is simply created using `rlang::error_cnd()`, things work just fine.

  paste(NextMethod(), "with_trace", sep = "\n")

title: update rlang on CRAN
description:
Hi.

I've discovered that rmarkdown on CRAN depends on the current dev version of rlang (0.4.11.9000), while rlang version on CRAN is 0.4.11. This is wrecking all sorts of havocs for new installs, where rmarkdown will fail to install because the correct rlang version is not available on CRAN. And rmarkdown being a pivotal package, this quite difficult to resolve neatly. 

It's mentioned in this ticket on the remotes package: https://github.com/r-lib/remotes/issues/610

Jim says it'll be resolved once the binaries are in place, and I'm assuming he's right. But I thought I'd make a note of it here that there is a dependency mismatch on CRAN for these two packages.

What do you think about adding a dynamic dots implementation of the built-in `switch`?

Below is a simple implementation with some examples.
``` r
switch2 <- function(
    expression_,
    ...
) {
    expression_ <- list(expression_)
    dots <- rlang::list2(...)

    do.call(switch, c(expression_, dots))

a <- "a"

title: Deparsing API
description:
Meta-issue about the deparsing API:

**Naming**

* I'm not sure why we duplicated the API with `expr_` and `quo_` functions. Isn't it simpler to just treat quosures as any other language type and deal with them in `expr_` functions as well?

* Perhaps relevant for naming: These functions are about pretty printing, while `expr_deparse()` is about transferring R objects as text. Though the latter also has pretty printing features such as omitting the last *n* elements of vectors.

* The naming of `expr_text()`, `expr_name()` etc generally suggests they are accessors. In reality they are actions (deparse variants).

* Are `expr_name()` and `quo_name()` misnomers? It seems it should only be used to provide default names for quoted arguments that might be complex expressions. I often see it used for transforming symbols to strings, which should better be done with `as_string()` or `as.character()` (the former works better on Windows with foreign characters).

    Perhaps `expr_pretty_name()` would be more suggestive that it's about default names?


**Features**

* Do we need a `_line()` variant? We are using `_name()` for backtraces, it seems we are really after line. title: feature request: signalers' message argument to auto-extract conditionMessage
description:
I find every now and then I use this 're-throw' condition pattern, typically from inside some specialized handler or class:
```r

  some_code_here()
}, error = function(e) {
  # perhaps log an error here, e.g. to stderr
  rlang::abort(conditionMessage(e), class = "special_error_subclass") ## or warn, inform, signal, etc.
})
```
... where the external caller then is equipped to handle different unique error subclasses, and each time for the condition message I have to `conditionMessage(original_condition_obj)`.

I'm curious to hear your thoughts on this feature request: let rlang's condition signalers' `message` argument auto-extract `conditionMessage(message)` if `message` is already a condition object?
So, in the above code, the re-throw line would look like `rlang::abort(e, class = "special_error_subclass")`.

Current behavior errs:
```r
rlang::abort(errorCondition("my msg"))
# Error in format_error_bullets(x[-1]) :

```

title: Offer a shortcut for eval_tidy(enquo(x))?
description:
For new users test-driving tidy evaluation (e.g. the `{{}}` mustaches), it would help to have a shortcut that operates like a quoting function. What would be a good name for `eval_tidy_quo()`?

``` r
library(rlang)

eval_tidy_quo <- function(expr, data = NULL, env = caller_env()) {
  eval_tidy(enquo(expr), data = data, env = env)
}

b <- 5
a <- sym("b")

# This is not tidy evaluation, a is unquoted eagerly?
eval_tidy({{a}})
#> [1] 5
eval_tidy(a)
#> [1] 5
eval_tidy({{a}}, data = list(b = 3))
#> [1] 3
eval_tidy(a, data = list(b = 3))
#> [1] 3

# Tidy evaluation without mustache:
eval_tidy_quo(a)
#> b

# Not picking up b from .GlobalEnv here
try(eval_tidy_quo({{a}}))
#> Error in eval_tidy(enquo(expr), data = data, env = env) : 
#>   object 'b' not found

# ...but works with the data mask
eval_tidy_quo({{a}}, data = list(b = 3))
#> [1] 3

# A quosure works
a <- quo(b)
eval_tidy_quo({{a}})
#> [1] 5

# Mustaches implement quote-unquote in a function:
quoting_fun <- function(expr) {
  eval_tidy_quo({{expr}})
}

quoting_fun(a)
#> <quosure>
#> expr: ^b
#> env:  global
quoting_fun({{a}})
#> [1] 5
```

title: Think of a better name for {{ }}
description:
The [quasiquotation help page](https://github.com/r-lib/rlang/blob/master/R/quasiquotation.R#L29-L31) calls `{{ }}` "interpolation", but that's a little confusing because interpolation has another, more common, meaning (it's what `approx()` does).

The [internal code](https://github.com/r-lib/rlang/blob/master/src/internal/expr-interp.c#L305-L308) calls `{{ }}` "curly-curly", but 4 syllables is too much to say out loud, and risks being shortened to "curlies", which is borderline rude.

So I think it's worth trying to come up with a better name before a bad one sticks.

This is hard, but here are a few possibilities to get started thinking about it.

### Synonyms for surrogate

Since the behavior of the operator is a bit like `substitute()`, it's worth thinking of [synonyms for that word](https://www.thesaurus.com/browse/substitute).

I quite like "surrogate", but "relief" and "broker" are other options.

### Words related to scoping

Since the point of the operation is to change the scope of where the variable is being evaluated, "rescope" might work. "Enclose" is another possibility which nicely sounds like "enquo".

### Words related to relocation

On a similar note, "migrate" or "transplant" help focus the attention on the fact the you're moving a variable from one environment to another.

### Words related to quoting

Since the operation does quoting and unquoting, a word related to quoting might be appropriate. Perhaps "retell" or "recollect". I also really like "parrot", which feels memorable.

### Wording related to finding

You could use an analogy of this operator finding variables. Most of the appropriate words already have some other meaning, but I quite like "sniff" and "ferret".

### Wording that describe the shape

Although curly-curly is cumbersome to say, it does make it clear what you are supposed to type. One quicker-to-say alternative is "seagulls", since a curly brace looks a bit like a seagull.

I'm out of ideas for now, but I'm sure there are more.

title: Register variables and data mask in eval_tidy()

These would be dynamically scoped, à-la tidyselect. Tidyselect would eventually use the variables registered with `eval_tidy()`, or share the same mechanism.

* Need a way to update the current vars, e.g. when ordering changes?

* `eval_tidy()` would just register the names of input data. When input is a mask, the creator must store the variables in the mask.

These dynamically scoped variables will support tidyselect, the new `acts()` and `sels()` helpers for creating data frames, and the new colwise helpers which will also return data frames.

title: rlang still calls deprecated as_character internally (eg. in as_utf8_character)
description:
**Observation:**

`rlang` has deprecated the function `as_character`

https://github.com/r-lib/rlang/blob/51f5cbde84797eeb6064a13d72eef1d7ed752502/R/lifecycle-retired.R#L322

https://github.com/r-lib/rlang/blob/e7500d4c5ca38c07607855a726961d8cf635bb9c/R/utils-encoding.R#L41

**Impact:**

If I call an `rlang` function it throws a warning for another internally called `rlang` function
even though the client never calls the deprecated function directly:

```
library(rlang)
options(lifecycle_disable_warnings = FALSE, lifecycle_verbose_soft_deprecation = TRUE)
rlang::as_utf8_character("abc")
```

shows

```
[1] "abc"
Warning message:
`as_character()` is deprecated as of rlang 0.4.0
Please use `vctrs::vec_cast()` instead.
This warning is displayed once per session. 
```

**Expected behaviour:**

Do not throw deprecation warnings when `rlang` package functions call other deprecated `rlang` functions.

Mainly: Replace all internal `as_character` calls with `vctrs::vec_cast` calls (as proposed by the deprecation message).

is_character(x) && all(x %in% values)
```

 I think this could be a useful addition to `rlang`'s family of fast `is_*` predicates, either as an additional argument to `is_character*()` family or maybe as an entirely new `is_factorish()` function. 

If the authors of `rlang` are interested in this functionality, I can provide an initial C implementation.

title: %|% is too strict about type for a length 1 input
description:
I just tried to use `%|%` for a scalar and got an error because the incoming `NA` is logical (as most are) and the scalar replacement value is character. It feels like our general policy is not to take the logical-ness of `NA` too literally in these situations.

It feels like this should work without me specifically ensuring `NA_character_`, which is often out of one's control.

``` r
library(rlang)

possibly_missing_scalar <- NA

possibly_missing_scalar %|% "fallback"
#> Error: Replacement values must have type logical, not type character

possibly_missing_scalar <- NA_character_

possibly_missing_scalar %|% "fallback"
#> [1] "fallback"
```

title: Attributes persist across calls to `rlang::quos`
description:
I'm developing a package that uses `rlang::quos` to provide some core functionality. 

When testing that package on R devel, I found that `rlang::quos` will create `<list_of<quosure>>` with attributes from the last `<list_of<quosure>>` object that was modified. 

### R (devel; using `rocker/tidyverse:devel`)

```r
> R.version.string
[1] "R Under development (unstable) (2021-02-19 r80028)"
> packageVersion("rlang")
[1] ‘0.4.10’
> x <- rlang::quos(a)
> attr(x, "test") <- "test attribute for object 'x'"
> y <- rlang::quos(b)
> y
<list_of<quosure>>

[[1]]
<quosure>
expr: ^b
env:  global

attr(,"test")
[1] "test attribute for object 'x'"
```

### R (4.0.3; using `rocker/tidyverse:latest`)

```r
> R.version.string
[1] "R version 4.0.3 (2020-10-10)"
> packageVersion("rlang")
[1] ‘0.4.10’
> x <- rlang::quos(a)
> attr(x, "test") <- "test attribute for object 'x'"
> y <- rlang::quos(b)
> y
<list_of<quosure>>

[[1]]
<quosure>
expr: ^b
env:  global
```

I don't expect experimental and developing packages to have completely stable APIs, but I felt like this might be of interest while working toward the next R release. It would help, though, to know whether this is functionality that `rlang` aims to provide or whether I should find another way of capturing this data that doesn't rely on attributes.

title: Why is `env_unlock()` dangerous?
description:
Motivation: In some languages, objects can be extended by way of adding methods. In R6, you can do this with unlocked objects. But, there is no way to restrict this: Once you have an unlocked object, you can just keep adding.

My idea is to use locked objects, extensible only by a limited set of decorators. These would have the ability to unlock the objects temporarily, add methods, re-assign their environments to make self/private work, lock the new bindings, and finally lock the environment. Using `rlang::env_unlock()` seems like a perfect solution here, given there is no base counterpart to `lockEnvironment()`.

But I see the docs are warning against this function ("should only be used in development tools or interactively") and [Lionel commented](https://github.com/r-lib/rlang/issues/423#issuecomment-369006924) the function might get removed from rlang altogether. I can implement it without rlang, but I am interested to hear your opinion on the approach I described above. Do you think unlocking object environments could be dangerous? And do you see this function ever being promoted to stable?

Any comments much appreciated, and many thanks for your continued work for the R community!

title: Defusing numbered dots
description:
This should capture `foo`:

```r
f <- function(...) enquo(..1)
f(foo)
#> Error in (function (arg)  : object '..1' not found
```

When `match.call()` matches dots, it creates numbered dots like `..1` or `..2`. Currently `enquo()` and `enquos()` don't handle these. This makes it difficult to use call-matching idioms which are sometimes useful (I think call-matching would be helpful to solve tidyverse/dplyr#5815).

```r
defuser <- function(...) enquos(...)


### Expected output

wrapper <- function(...) {
  foo <- 1
  defuser(..., y = foo)
}
local({
  bar <- 10
  wrapper(x = bar)
})
#> <list_of<quosure>>
#>
#> $x
#> <quosure>
#> expr: ^bar
#> env:  0x7fa13f27b040
#>
#> $y
#> <quosure>
#> expr: ^foo
#> env:  0x7fa13f27add8


### Problematic output

wrapper2 <- function(...) {
  foo <- 1
  eval(match.call(
    defuser,
    quote(defuser(..., y = foo)),
    envir = environment()
  ))
}
local({
  bar <- 10
  wrapper2(x = bar)
})
#> <list_of<quosure>>
#>
#> $x
#> <quosure>
#> expr: ^..1
#> env:  0x7fa1488cb438
#>
#> $y
#> <quosure>
#> expr: ^foo
#> env:  0x7fa1488cb438
```

title: `enquo()` does not play well with magrittr pipe
description:
The following function takes the unquoted name of a package and returns the package name as a string:
```
get_pkg_name_v1 <- function(pkg) {
  pkg <- rlang::enquo(pkg)
  rlang::quo_name(pkg)
}
get_pkg_name_v1(rlang)
# [1] "rlang"
```
and this works smoothly.

However if I try rewriting the same function using **magrittr**'s pipe operator, things go sideways:
```
get_pkg_name_v2 <- function(pkg) {
  pkg %>% 
    rlang::enquo() %>% 
    rlang::quo_name()
}
get_pkg_name_v2(rlang)
# [1] "pkg"
```

It seems that it is `enquo()` that does not play well with the pipe because the following version works well:
```
get_pkg_name_v3 <- function(pkg) {
  pkg <- rlang::enquo(pkg)
  pkg %>% 
    rlang::quo_name()
}
get_pkg_name_v3(rlang)
# [1] "rlang"
```

title: Add support for sentinel values
description:
`ggplot2` has built in sentinel value support using the `waiver()` function: https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/blob/9741da5050f81b7b5c012c56d02f45fc93d68f89/R/utilities.r#L177-L188

```r
#' A waiver object.
#'
#' A waiver is a "flag" object, similar to `NULL`, that indicates the
#' calling function should just use the default value.  It is used in certain
#' functions to distinguish between displaying nothing (`NULL`) and
#' displaying a default value calculated elsewhere (`waiver()`)
#'
#' @export
#' @keywords internal
waiver <- function() structure(list(), class = "waiver")

is.waive <- function(x) inherits(x, "waiver")
```

I've run into a situation a few times where I can **not** use `NULL` as a placeholder value for an argument as `NULL` could be supplied by a user and should be used. 
Using `missing(arg)` does not allow for other functions to build on top of my function as the arguments might be directly supplied, which makes `missing()` not very useful.

`ggplot2` resolved this situation by supplying a `waiver()` function which allows for users to supply `NULL` values and can be distinguished from default behavior.

------------------------

I think it would be great if there was a "sentinel" value that can be validated it is a sentinel value.

I am opening this issue for discussion and would be happy to make a PR. Thank you!

title: `env_print` returns `lazy` for bindings, if the function hasn't been evaluated
description:
To reproduce
```r
library("rlang")

power1 <- function(exp) {
  function(x) {
    x ^ exp
  }
}
square <- power1(2)

env_print(square)
#> <environment: 0x558cab2d3c70>
#> parent: <environment: global>
#> bindings:
#>  * exp: <lazy>

square(1)
env_print(square)
#> <environment: 0x558cab2d3c70>
#> parent: <environment: global>
#> bindings:
#>  * exp: <dbl>
```

This behavior is not documented in the documentation.
We should either document this, or make sure `env_print` returns the underlying type of all bindings.

title: testing missing values when passing from parent function
description:
I'm struggling to test/evaluate missing values when these are passed on from a parent function. This is due to the laziness of argument evaluation. Below is a small example 

``` r
library(rlang, warn.conflicts = F)
library(purrr, warn.conflicts = F)

f <- function(a, b, c, d) {
   args <- call_args(match.call())
   do.call(sum, args)
}

g <- function(a, b, c, d) {
  f(a, b, c, d)
}

f(1,2,3,4)
#> [1] 10
g(1,2,3,4)
#> [1] 10
f(1,2,3)
#> [1] 6
g(1,2,3)
#> Error in f(a, b, c, d): argument "d" is missing, with no default

# `match.call()` collects the lazy arguments so it is not helpful
f <- function(a, b, c, d) {
  args <- call_args(match.call())
  cat("args:", paste(names(args), "=", args, collapse = ", "), "\n")
  miss <- map(args, is_missing)
  cat("miss:", paste(names(miss), "=", miss, collapse = ", "), "\n")
  args <- args[!unlist(miss)]
  do.call(sum, args)
}

f(1,2,3)
#> args: a = 1, b = 2, c = 3 
#> miss: a = FALSE, b = FALSE, c = FALSE
#> [1] 6
g(1,2,3)
#> args: a = a, b = b, c = c, d = d 
#> miss: a = FALSE, b = FALSE, c = FALSE, d = FALSE
#> Error in f(a, b, c, d): argument "d" is missing, with no default


# the missing argument can be handled inside the function with `is_missing()`
# but his can be counter productive if you have a lot of these kind of functions and/or arguments
f <- function(a, b, c, d) {
  args <- call_args(match.call())
  cat("args:", paste(names(args), "=", args, collapse = ", "), "\n")
  if(is_missing(c)) args$c <- NULL
  if(is_missing(d)) args$d <- NULL
  do.call(sum, args)
}

f(1,2)
#> args: a = 1, b = 2
#> [1] 3
g(1,2)
#> args: a = a, b = b, c = c, d = d
#> [1] 3

# any attempt to "automate" (make dynamic) the detection of missing values fails
f <- function(a, b, c, d) {
  args <- call_args(match.call())
  cat("args:", paste(names(args), "=", args, collapse = ", "), "\n")
  e <- current_env()
  miss <- map(names(args), ~{is_missing(e[[.x]])})
  args <- args[!unlist(miss)]
  do.call(sum, args)
}

f(1)
#> args: a = 1
#> [1] 1
g(1)
#> args: a = a, b = b, c = c, d = d
#> Error in f(a, b, c, d): argument "b" is missing, with no default
traceback() # added manually since reprex does not support this
#> 5: is_missing(e[[.x]])
#> 4: .f(.x[[i]], ...)
#> 3: map(names(args), ~is_missing(e[[.x]])) at #6
#> 2: f(a, b, c, d) at #2
#> 1: g(1)
```

My question: Is there a set of existing or future tools in `rlang` that would help with this particular problem?

title: set_attrs() API
description:
I think `set_attrs()` should not update part of the attributes, it should update the attributes as a whole. Then `add_attrs()` would be used to update the attributes. Maybe also have `poke_attrs()` and `push_attrs()` variants that would change the attributes in place. This generally only makes sense in C code but it's nice to be able to prototype with R.

Same for `set_class()` vs `add_class()`.

Maybe it'd also makes sense to have some kind of "matcher" argument for `add_` and `push_` functions? Or/and offset?

title: Tests for visibility of as_function()
description:
I just spent a few hours trying to figure out why my tests were passing locally but failing in CI. It turns out the dev version of `as_function()` preserves visibility, but the CRAN version does not.

This is good, but to ensure it stays good, I suggest adding tests like these:

```R
f <- as_function(quo(invisible(1)))
expect_invisible(f())

f <- as_function(quo(1))
expect_visible(f())

f <- as_function(~ invisible(1))
expect_invisible(f())

f <- as_function(~ 1)
expect_visible(f())
```

These fail on the CRAN version, but pass on the dev version.

The original problem is probably related to #961.

expected behaviour of sym / enexpr
description:
Maybe this is not how these functions are supposed to be used, but is this behaviour as expected? `sym` seems to have a side effect such that subsequent calls on the same parameter are affected.

``` r
library(rlang)

test_enexpr_sym <- function(s1) {
  list(enexpr(s1),
       sym(s1))
}

test_sym_enexpr <- function(s1) {
  list(sym(s1),
       enexpr(s1))
}

one <- "two"
test_enexpr_sym(one)
#> [[1]]
#> one
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> two
test_sym_enexpr(one)
#> [[1]]
#> two
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] "two"
```

title: Backtrace truncated
description:
There is a limit for the length of the error message, the default is 1000 characters, and it can be set higher, but the max is 8192. Since the trace is printed as part of the error message, this means that the trace can be truncated, which is especially not great in non-interactive sessions. E.g.

``` r
cat(deparse(substitute({
  ff <- lapply(1:10, function(i) {
    assign(
      paste0("f", i), function() do.call(paste0("f", i-1), list()),
      envir = .GlobalEnv)
  })
  
  f0 <- function() rlang::abort("oops")
  
  f10()
})), file = tmp <- tempfile(), sep = "\n")

out <- processx::run("R", c("-q", "-f", tmp))
cat(out$stderr)
#> Error: oops
#> Backtrace:
#>      █

title: Implications of is_interactive() consulting the option "rstudio.notebook.executing"
description: I use `rlang::is_interactive()` in gargle (and many other places). gargle may need to interact with the user, for example, initially it will ask the user for permission to create a token cache. Or, in regular usage, gargle may offer the user a menu of different emails to select from when auth-ing with a specific API. If a user likes to work in R Notebooks or in regular Rmd's with the "Chunk output inline" behaviour, this interacts very poorly with `rlang::is_interactive()`, which reports `FALSE` for them, even though they are in an interactive session. Or, at least, the user certainly _thinks_ they are in an interactive session. Is something you've run up against / thought about before? I am thinking I might just have to counsel people to NOT use "Chunk output inline" with gargle-using packages. Or they have to code their script as if they are in a non-interactive session.

title: Improve display of chained errors
description:
```r
a <- function() b()
b <- function() c()
c <- function() abort("low-level")

f <- function() g()
g <- function() h()
h <- function() tryCatch(a(), error = function(err) abort("high-level", parent = err))

f()
#> Error: high-level
#> Call `rlang::last_error()` to see a backtrace.

last_error()
#> <error/rlang_error>
#> high-level
#> Backtrace:
#>  1. global::f()
#>  2. global::g()
#>  3. global::h()
#> Call `rlang::last_trace()` to see the full backtrace.

last_trace()
#> <error/rlang_error>
#> high-level
#> Backtrace:
#>     █
#>  1. └─global::f()
#>  2.   └─global::g()
#>  3.     └─global::h()
#> <parent: error/rlang_error>
#> low-level
#> Backtrace:
#>     █
#>  1. └─global::a()
#>  2.   └─global::b()
#>  3.     └─global::c()

last_error()$parent
#> <error/rlang_error>
#> low-level
#> Backtrace:
#>   1. global::f()
#>   2. global::g()
#>   3. global::h()
#>   8. global::a()
#>   9. global::b()
#>  10. global::c()

last_error()$parent$trace
#>      █
#>   1. └─global::f()
#>   2.   └─global::g()
#>   3.     └─global::h()
#>   4.       ├─base::tryCatch(...)
#>   5.       │ └─base:::tryCatchList(expr, classes, parentenv, handlers)
#>   6.       │   └─base:::tryCatchOne(expr, names, parentenv, handlers[[1L]])
#>   7.       │     └─base:::doTryCatch(return(expr), name, parentenv, handler)
#>   8.       └─global::a()
#>   9.         └─global::b()
#>  10.           └─global::c()
```


Comments from @gaborcsardi 

1. It would make sense to indicate in the default output that there is another level. Even the last_error() output does not indicate that, actually. You probably end up staring at the error for a bit and then calling last_error() as suggested, and then after some more staring last_trace(), as suggested. And you'd better not mistype either one, because then the last error object will be gone.

2. Having to call $parent to get a complete stack is not great, especially if you have more than two levels, i.e. last_error()$parent$parent, etc. The same with last_error()$parent$parent$trace, etc.

3. Having different numbers for the parent frames in last_trace() might be confusing. Personally I would prefer if the numbers were not mangled, and they referred to the real frame numbers.

4. There is no way to see all error messages and a full stack, in the same output. Personally, this is my preferred output, as above, as it shows all information, and the levels are clearly separated by whitespace, and they are easy to parse. I can decide how deep I need to dig into the output, without issuing additional commands.

5. Relatedly, I am not sure that having all these different kinds of output is great. People need to learn to parse all of them, and think about whether the information they are looking for is missing in general, or they need the other kind of output, etc.

expr: ^test
env:  package:base
```
