title: tildes in quosures
description:
This seems odd to me (rlang 0.4.4).

``` r
library(rlang)
`~` <- function(...) stop('boom')
~ 1 + 1
#> Error in ~1 + 1: boom
x <- quo(~1 + 1)
eval_tidy(x)
#> ~1 + 1
#> <environment: 0x7f9bca6eea00>
```

Two unexpected things:

1. My overloaded tilde is ignored
2. The returned formula doesn't have .GlobalEnv as its environment (note this is true even when run without reprex).

My mental model of how this all works is incomplete, but I feel it should be possible fetch the correct tilde to evaluate in `base_tilde_eval` with `findVar` (in function finding mode anyway, if it does such thing like `get` does), instead of just going directly to the primitive.  Obviously a pretty unlikely corner case to hit (if indeed I'm even correct about this being an error).

Not sure what's going on with the environment.  Feels like `quo_env` should be the global environment here?  Or is that still some kind of mask env even without data?

description:
rlang encourages interfaces that handle unevaluated expressions and names.

Yet rlang’s `.data` pronoun can only be subset with strings, not names. This is inconsistent, and [leads people to perform metaprogramming with strings, rather than with quosures](https://www.reddit.com/r/rstats/comments/ca90nk/why_i_love_datatable/et8y42i/).

Unfortunately metaprogramming still scares people (see linked discussion thread), and I believe that making `.data` subsetting work with names would simplify many common use-cases (this is only partially alleviated by the new `{{…}}` interpolation syntax, which only works with unevaluated function arguments), and would encourage use of R language objects over strings for metaprogramming.

(The next logical step would be for the documentation to *discourage* using `.data` with strings, but here I’m getting ahead of myself.)

To clarify what I’m talking about, this is a request to make the following code legal:

```r
var1 = quote(weight)
dplyr::summarize(ChickWeight, mean(.data[[var1]]))

var2 = quo(weight)
dplyr::summarize(ChickWeight, mean(.data[[var2]]))
```

title: `is_true` (and `is_false`) defined too strictly?
description:
rlang's [`is_true`](https://github.com/r-lib/rlang/blob/e7500d4c5ca38c07607855a726961d8cf635bb9c/R/types.R#L294) (and `is_false`) are defined how base R's _previous_ `isTRUE` and `isFALSE` were defined.

In more recent R versions, `isTRUE` has been modified to not fail in certain situations (e.g. a _named_ logical scalar of length one with `TRUE` as the value) ... should rlang's version be changed to this less-strict (and, I'd argue, more intuitive, _especially_ for new programmers) definition?

Here's base R's current definition of `isTRUE` and the corresponding documentation for the change:
```R
isTRUE <- function (x) {
  is.logical(x) && length(x) == 1L && !is.na(x) && x
}
```
> In earlier R versions, ‘isTRUE <- function(x) identical(x, TRUE)’, had the drawback to be false e.g., for ‘x <- c(val = TRUE)’.

title: Suggestion: Preserve expression names in `parse_exprs()`
description:
This is a very minor suggestion, but the current behavior of `parse_exprs` does not preserve expression names if given a named string vector.

``` r
x <- parse_exprs( c(e1="a+b", e2="a*10") )
# [[1]]
# a + b
#
# [[2]]
# a * 10
```

The desired behavior can be emulated via `purrr::map()` as
``` r
y <- purrr::map( c(e1="a+b", e2="a*10"), parse_expr )
# $e1
# a + b
# 
# $e2
# a * 10
```

The motivation for this is to help streamline downstream usage in `dplyr` verbs. For example,

``` r
tibble( a=1:3, b=4:6 ) %>% mutate( !!!y )
# # A tibble: 3 x 4
#       a     b    e1    e2
#   <int> <int> <int> <dbl>
# 1     1     4     5    10
# 2     2     5     7    20
# 3     3     6     9    30
```
produces columns with desired names `e1` and `e2`, whereas the equivalent `mutate( !!!x )` doesn't.

title: Side effect bug when using quosures
description:
I'm writing a function where I need to check if my enquoted first argument is a lambda function (it could be pretty much anything else).

Therefore, I ended using this piece of code to test this condition:

```r
library(rlang)
foo = function(.vars=NULL) {
    x = enquo(.vars) #this line is mandatory, due to other code in the function
    is_lambda(as_function(quo_squash(x)))
}
foo(~mean(.x)>3.5)
```
Unfortunately, `as_function` throws the following error:

> Error: `env` must be an environment

I tried a lot of things, using `set_env` on almost all objects, but the only thing that could prevent this error was to use `try`:

```r
bar = function(.vars=NULL) {
    dummy_variable_ill_never_ever_use = try(.vars, silent = T)
    x = enquo(.vars)
    is_lambda(as_function(quo_squash(x)))
}
bar(~mean(.x)>3.5)
```

Actually, the assignment is optional, but the point is that the `try` call has a side-effect that somehow prevents the error.

I thought it could be due to my computer, but testing on https://rdrr.io/snippets/ gave the exact same behavior.

Here is some more info on the error:

title: Add `eval_tidy()` version with default
description:
In ggplot2, we extensively use the pattern `<data> %||% <default value>`, as in `color <- data$color %||% "red"`. This works great when we know what column we want to look up in the data frame, but it fails if we want to do this with `eval_tidy()`, because `eval_tidy()` fails instead of returning `NULL`.

In my own code, I've worked around this by defining a function `eval_default()` which works like `eval_tidy()` but swaps in a default value if `eval_tidy()` fails:
https://github.com/wilkelab/cowplot/blob/06aeeb449ccc0fb343eb03c83111df7b171e73af/R/key_glyph.R#L145-L154

``` r
library(rlang)

eval_default <- function(x, data, default) {
  force(default)
  
  suppressWarnings(
    tryCatch(
      error = function(e) default,
      eval_tidy(x, data)
    )
  )
}

data <- data.frame(x = 1)
eval_default(quo(x), data, NULL)
#> [1] 1
eval_default(quo(y), data, NULL)
#> NULL
```

<sup>Created on 2020-01-12 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

Based on the conversation [here,](https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/issues/2963#issuecomment-573441165) it seems I'm not the only one running into this issue, so maybe adding something like this function to rlang is justified.

One comment regarding my proposed implementation: I had to add `suppressWarnings()` to prevent a warning "restarting interrupted promise evaluation" that would sometimes pop up. I find this warning sufficiently disconcerting that I'm not sure I can just ignore it, but I don't know enough about the internals of R evaluation to understand what the warning means and whether it can be avoided instead of suppressed.

title: enquos() and friends should warn if ... contains arguments that start with a dot
description:
Functions that use `...` as dynamic dots generally use arguments that start with a dot for options. We rely on user's discipline to avoid objects that start with a dot.

If users/developers accidentally/deliberately use arguments that start with a dot, they expose themselves to the risk of breaking changes when we introduce an option that has the same name.

Should we be more strict here, and warn/err/strip optionally?

``` r
library(rlang)

# Implementation sketch for better list2()
list3 <- function(...) {
  oldskool <- enexprs(..., .unquote_names = FALSE)
  out <- list2(...)

  tidy_names <- (names2(oldskool) != names2(out))
  starts_with_dot <- grepl("^[.]", names(out))

  bad <- !tidy_names & starts_with_dot
  if (any(bad)) {
    warn("Use := or !!! for arguments that start with a dot.")
    out <- out[!bad]
  }
  out
}

my_dots_1 <- function(...) {
  list3(...)
}

my_dots_2 <- function(..., .dot = FALSE) {
  print(.dot)
  list3(...)
}

my_dots_1(.dot = "bogus")
#> Warning: Use := or !!! for arguments that start with a dot.
#> named list()
my_dots_1(.dot := "bogus")
#> $.dot
#> [1] "bogus"
# FIXME: How to handle this case?
my_dots_1(!!!list(.dot = "bogus"))
#> Warning: Use := or !!! for arguments that start with a dot.
#> named list()

my_dots_2(.dot = "bogus")
#> [1] "bogus"
#> list()
my_dots_2(.dot := "bogus")
#> [1] FALSE
#> $.dot
#> [1] "bogus"
# FIXME: How to handle this case?
my_dots_2(!!!list(.dot = "bogus"))
#> [1] FALSE
#> Warning: Use := or !!! for arguments that start with a dot.
#> named list()
```

title: sys.parent Stymied by Mask Environment
description:
The mask environment used to store the tilde is not placed on the context stack.  This prevents `sys.parent` from functioning correctly.  When nested inside a closure, `sys.parent` will get stuck at the closure frame evaluated in the mask environment.  This is because that closure runs with `cptr->sysparent` as the mask environment, and when that doesn't exist on the stack [`R_sysparent` gets stuck at that context][1]:

```
eval_tidy(quo((function() sys.parent(10))()))
## [1] 2
eval(quote((function() sys.parent(10))()))
## [1] 0
```

This also appears affects `call_frame`.

When there is no intervening closure then, the [logic that tries to unwind the `sys.*`][2] frame prior to looking for parents causes those functions to blow past all the frames because it's looking for the mask environment on the call stack:

```
eval_tidy(
  quo(
    (function()
      (function()
        (function() !!quo(sys.parent(1)))()
      )()
    )()
  )
)
## [1] 0
eval(
  quote(
    (function()
      (function()
        (function() eval(quote(sys.parent(1))))()
      )()
    )()
  )
)
## [1] 6
```
[1]: https://github.com/wch/r-source/blob/tags/R-4-0-0/src/main/context.c#L432
[2]: https://github.com/wch/r-source/blob/tags/R-4-0-0/src/main/context.c#L632

title: Pronouns in Package development
description:
The following function
```
dot_func <- function(x)
{
  x %>%
    paste0("hello ",.)
}
```
outputs as you would expect:
```
> dot_func("world")
[1] "hello world"
```

However, it gives a Note when `devtools::check()` is ran:
```
> checking R code for possible problems ... NOTE
  dot_func: no visible binding for global variable '.'
  Undefined global functions or variables:
    .
```

The [documentation ](https://rlang.r-lib.org/reference/tidyeval-data.html) for data pronouns suggests replacing `.` with `.data`, doing this stops the Note:
```
dot_func2 <- function(x)
{
  x %>%
    paste0("hello ",.data)
}
```
```
0 errors √ | 0 warnings √ | 0 notes √
```
however, the output is incorrect:
```
> dot_func2("world")
[1] "worldhello "
```
This is because the `.data` pronoun is designed for extracting elements of `data.frames` and `magrittr` doesn't substitute the `.data` in the same way it does with `.`. It is essentially running `paste0(x,"hello ",.data)`, rather than the desired `paste0("hello ",x)`.

A solution I have found is to define `.` as a fake pronoun in the same way that `.data` (and `.env`) are defined.
```
. <-  structure(list(), class = "rlang_fake_data_pronoun")
```

However, I'd like some advice as to whether others think this could potentially cause problems as I'm not 100% sure of the ramifications. In theory, any use of `.` within a function or pipeline should be replaced appropriately, but would this cover up error alerts if `.` is missing? 

Is there a better solution that would be recommended and would eliminate this `devtools::check()` Note? I find it difficult to understand why I've found it so hard to find this solution if it is fine.

Is there a reason this *wasn't* done in `rlang`? If not, would it make a reasonable PR to add this to `eval_tidy()`?

title: splice enexpr(arg) as list into downstream call
description:
Suppose I want to capture multiple arguments (e.g. with `enexpr`) that themselves are argument lists for downstream calls, is there a good way to do that?

This dummy snippet kinda works, but feels hackish, and bound to break...

```r
hack <- function(x, f1_args, f2_args){
  f1_exprs <- as.list(enexpr(f1_args))[-1]
  f2_exprs <- as.list(enexpr(f2_args))[-1]

  filter(x, !!! f1_exprs) %>%
    select(!!! f2_exprs)
}

df <- tibble(x=1:3, y=4)
hack(df, c(x>1), c(y, z=x))
```

title: Problems using quosures with data.table
description:
I think this is an rlang issue, but I could be wrong.

I'm trying to create a summarize-like function using quosures and data.table. Everything works fine unless I try to add a "by" to the data.table expression.

``` r
library(data.table)
library(rlang)
library(magrittr)

summarize_no_by <- function(.df, ...) {

  dots <- enquos(...)
  
  dt_quo <- quo(
    .df[, list(!!!dots)]
  )

  eval_tidy(dt_quo, .df)
}

summarize_with_by <- function(.df, ..., .by = NULL) {

  dots <- enquos(...)
  .by <- enquo(.by)
  
  dt_quo <- quo(
    .df[, list(!!!dots), by = !!.by]
  )

  eval_tidy(dt_quo, .df)
}

test_df <- data.table(x = 1:3, y = c("a", "a", "b"))

# Works
test_df %>%
  summarize_no_by(avg_x = mean(x))
#>    avg_x
#> 1:     2

# Fails
test_df %>%
  summarize_with_by(avg_x = mean(x), .by = y)
#> Error: Base operators are not defined for quosures.
#> Do you need to unquote the quosure?
#> 
#>   # Bad:
#>   myquosure == rhs
#> 
#>   # Good:
#>   !!myquosure == rhs
```

This example works fine using `enexprs()` instead of `enquos()`, but I have a use case that needs quosures to work correctly.

title: Able to use rlang::UQ() but not rlang::`!!`()
description:
For data analysis scripts, I often find that rlang is useful once or twice in the script, so I only want to use the exported functions rather than load the whole package.

One common use case is when I have a variable column name stored as a string and I want to use `!!sym(col_name)` so that I can perform an arbitrary operation such as `count(data, !!sym(col_name))`.

Without loading rlang, it's easy to do this using `rlang::UQ(rlang::sym(col_name))`. But at that moment we can't do the seemingly equivalent `` rlang::`!!`(rlang::sym(col_name)) ``. Here's a simple example:

    library(dplyr)

    col_name <- "Species"

    # This works
    select(iris, rlang::UQ(rlang::sym(col_name)))

    # This doesn't
    select(iris, rlang::`!!`(rlang::sym(col_name)))

Could the `` `!!`() `` function be updated to allow it to work without having to load rlang?

description:

I upgraded to R 4.0.0 this weekend. The new version of R also requires a new version of Rtools. Previously, Rtools was installed in c:/Rtools. The new Rtools is now installed in c:/rtools40. Most of my packages, including ones that needed to be installed from source, updated just fine, except rlang (and a couple other minor ones).

The error indicated that when trying to install "rlang" the install script was trying to look for the old version of Rtools in the c:/Rtools folder, which i had removed. (I wish I had copied the exact error, but it was something like "c:/Rtools/mingw_64/bin/gcc no such file or directory.") 

So reinstalled the old version of Rtools, but I still kept the new version too. Since they are in different folders it's not a problem (yet?!). I have the additional line in my .Renviron file that prepends the location of the new Rtools40 to the path, but I also added back the path to the old Rtools in my system settings (so not in .Renviron). Anyway, that worked: I was able to install rlang. 

I'm posting here in case other people run into the same problem and are looking for a (somewhat hackish) solution. Also, I was wondering if you might have any ideas why the install script might be looking for the old Rtools?

Thanks.

title: Require list-inputs in `flatten()`
description:
For example, we shouldn't be able to flatten a data frame:

```r
flatten(data.frame(x = 1))
#> $x
#> [1] 1
```

But this is slightly complex because we don't want to flatten `list_of` types, which are atomics. So we can't use `if (!inherits(x, "list")) {error}` as a check, because a `list_of` inherits from `"list"`.

On the other hand, there might be an argument for it to work with `list_of`, since `[[` on a `list_of` returns a different type, which is not a property of atomics. Also `list_of<list_of<>>` is recursive. If `flatten()` did work with S3 lists like this, it should probably return a `list_of` as well 

Hopefully explicitly checking for list input will provide a better error message for atomic vectors too

```r
flatten(1)
#> Error in flatten(1): VECTOR_ELT() can only be applied to a 'list', not a 'double'
```

Maybe an `abort()` could be used before we get here?

title: Review documentation about quoting
description:
Documentation of `expr` states:

```
        • ‘expr()’ returns its argument unevaluated. It is equivalent
          to ‘base::bquote()’.

        • ‘enexpr()’ takes an argument name and returns it unevaluated.
          It is equivalent to ‘base::substitute()’.
``` 

The "equivalence" is an overstatement. `expr` is not equivalent to `bquote` because it uses `!!` for unquoting instead of `.` and it doesn't allow for an explicit environment. At the most the doc should say "parallels" and provide further details.

The second parallel is even more confusing. It looks like `enexpr` is designed to be used only for function arguments inside functions.  `substitute` is more general than that. It evaluates symbols located in the supplied env which enexpr doesn't have.

```R
> local({a <- 1; substitute(a + 1)})
1 + 1
>  local({a <- 1; enexpr(a + 1)})
Error in (function (x, strict = TRUE)  (from utils.R#89) : "x" must be an argument name
> 
```

BTW, what's the rationale for the `enquo` and `enexpr` names in the first place>  If these are explicitly designed for arguments, wouldn't `argquo` and `argexpr` make more sense? Also, the relationship between `enexpr` and `expr` is not particularly clear. How would one write `enexpr` by means of `expr` alone?

title: Should `rlang::inform()` use `stdout()` by default?
description:
One issue with `base::message()` is that it outputs to `stderr()`, which while it works great for terminal usage, in RStudio and in the Windows GUI causes the output to be in red.

I just did a [workaround for this in vroom](https://github.com/r-lib/vroom/commit/55a94bb9dfd18eac30c4771f3c48dc6af6c55f86#diff-90a167c269c93fd663f1c3c690147343R460-R472). Maybe we should do this by default in `rlang::inform()`? 

Currently some packages (such as usethis) use `cat()` for user messaging to avoid the red text issue, but they really should use message conditions, so users can use `suppressMessages()` to suppress the messages.

title: Named arguments in lambda functions
description:
One limitation of rlang's lambda functions is the inability to specify argument names.  While this isn't a problem in most cases that anonymous functions are helpful, it makes lambdas less useful for `purrr::pmap()` and relatives.  I'm proposing an expansion of the lambda syntax that could allow argument names.

To specify arguments, `as_function()` should be passed a two-sided formula; the RHS is converted into the function body as usual, but the LHS is interpreted as the arguments with the following rules:

- Arguments can be declared directly with the pseudo-function f(), e.g. `f(a, b) ~ a + b`; this accepts forcing and splicing arguments.
- Arguments can be passed as a character vector, e.g., `c("d", "e") ~ d - e`
- Arguments can be taken from the names of a list or dataframe, e.g., `iris ~ Sepal.Length / Sepal.Width`

Multiple forms could be combined with the `+` operator (which could be useful if there are different 

The last option would be the easiest to use with `purrr::pmap()`:
```r
iris %>% pmap_chr(.l ~ Sepal.Length/Sepal.Width)
```
If the community is interested in this or has comments, I'd be happy to contribute the code and tests.

title: Minimum requirements are not enough for tests to pass
description:
When building against an older system, some tests fail:
```
  1. Error: error is printed with backtrace (@test-cnd-abort.R#80)
  2. Error: parent errors are not displayed in error message and backtrace (@test-cnd-abort.R#113)
  3. Error: backtrace reminder is displayed when called from `last_error()` (@test-cnd-abort.R#135)
  4. Error: capture context doesn't leak into low-level backtraces (@test-cnd-abort.R#178)
  5. Error: can use conditionMessage() method in subclasses of rlang errors (@test-cnd-error.R#22)
  6. Error: rlang_error.print() calls conditionMessage() method (@test-cnd-error.R#46)
```
Comparing to a system that does work, the differences seem to be:
```patch

+backports 1.1.5
+ellipsis 0.3.0
-htmltools 0.3.6
+htmltools 0.4.0
-pillar 1.3.1
+pillar 1.4.2
-testthat 2.0.1
+testthat 2.2.1
+vctrs 0.2.0
+zeallot 0.1.0
```
I'm not sure if it's new pillar or new testthat that is required. This is new with 0.4.1, I believe, as well.

title: Can we use sym() with a vector of strings?
description:
Hi,

I've been trying to solve a problem using tidyeval and encountered that sym can be used with either a string, or a list of strings, but weirdly not a vector of strings (or more precisely a named vector of strings). I think this would be a useful addition just using the same syntax of sym().

It may be helpful to describe the problem I've been trying to solve in order to understand the use of the vectors os strings at all, and it would be helpful just in case there is a much better way of solving my problem and the need for sym with a vector is invalid.

I'm working on a tibble of approximately 300,000 rows and 300 columns looking at stroke care (each row is a stroke patient admission). We have an initially large dataset that we then produce a series of calculated fields for (ie. summations or other calculations on the raw data). We then undertake a load of aggregated summary calculations to produce Key Indicators which are used in reports, with the data grouped by a team and a time period (eg. quarterly or monthly dependent on the report. Each Key Indicator is measured in two ways, one 'Patient Centred - PC', and one 'Team Centred - TC' result (a patient's stroke care can be delivered by multiple different teams so the team measures only the care delivered by that organisation whereas the patient measures record care delivered to any patient who comes in contact with a team, regardless of whether the team delivered it or not). So, PC and TC fields are paired - we usually either want a summary of just the TC fields, or of both TC and PC fields for other reports.

Some of the calculations are complex and need to be right, so I've structured the code to make unit testing easier into sets of indicators are grouped into domains. I've then used the quos command to construct a list of functions for each domain, which we then join together to carry out one giant mutate (for calculated fields) or summarise (for the aggregated values) in one go.

So for one of the domains, here is the function definitions, and the variable names set as strings (so bear in mind there will be another 8 or 9 files with further function definitions - many more complex than these):

d1ki_aggr_value_names <- c(
  kiclockstarttobrainimagingmins = "KIClockStartToBrainImagingMins",
  kibrainimagingwithin1hr = "KIBrainImagingWithin1hr",
  kibrainimagingwithin12hrs = "KIBrainImagingWithin12hrs")
  
d1ki_aggr_value_functions <- rlang::quos(
  KIMedianBrainImagingTime = median(
  !!d1ki_aggr_value_names["kiclockstarttobrainimagingmins"],
  na.rm = TRUE),
  KIPCScannedIn1Hr = nonNApercentage(
  !!d1ki_aggr_value_names["kibrainimagingwithin1hr"]),
  KIPCScannedIn12Hrs = nonNApercentage(
  !!d1ki_aggr_value_names["kibrainimagingwithin12hrs"]))

We join d1ki_aggr_value_functions to similar lists of functions, and perform a dplyr::summarise operation on the source data. For the unit tests, you create a minimal test set and perform just the one set of functions on the test set. So far so good.

Obviously names is starting life as a vector of named strings here. Each of the strings starting with 'KI' is actually the suffix of a pair of column names: TCKIClockStartToBrainImagingMins and PCKIClockStartToBrainImagingMins for example. My cunning plan was that we could append the prefix to the strings using paste0, then turn all the strings into symbols, merge the functions quos lists together for all the domains, and execute the summary for one or both of the pair of results. The purpose of having the vector of strings is hopefully therefore obvious from the example.

Of course then sym doesn't work on vectors so we'd have to loop through each one individually.

Firstly, is there a reason sym doesn't work on vectors of strings (or could it be something which could be implemented)? Secondly - are there any better suggestions for the implementation above?

title: Unquoting/unquote splicing inside purrr::map inside dplyr::mutate calls
description:
I'd like to be able to construct calls from columns of a dataframe. Background: I collect my model ingredients tidyly in a dataframe and expand this dataframe to hold all possible combinations, which I map over. However, sometimes I want call different functions with, again, different sets of parameters to calculate i.e. SEs. Unquote splicing doesn't seems to be straightforward when applied to such nested structures. Possibly related to the timing of evaluations and available environments.

Here is a simple reprex:

``` r
library(tidyverse)
library(rlang)

x <- tibble(a = letters[1:3],
            b = 1:3)

y <- tibble(args = list(list(NULL), list(sep = "->")),
       names = list("paste0", "paste"))

xy <- expand_grid(x, y)

xy <- xy %>%
  mutate(call = pmap(list(a, b, names, args), ~call2(..3, ..1, ..2, !!!..4)))
#> Error in splice(dot_call(capture_dots, frame_env = frame_env, named = named, : ..4 used in an incorrect context, no ... to look in
```

title: Feature request: f_rhs additional argumen to locate in relation to |
description:
Hi there,
Many formulas use `|` in their RHS. It is often useful to extract the part before a "|" or after. It would be a nice enhancement to add an argument to `f_rhs` like `n = 1` to return only the RHS before the first "|", or `n = 2` to return the next part of the RHS.

The [Formula package](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/Formula/Formula.pdf) accomplishes this, for example

    fml <- y ~ a + b | c + s
    library(Formula)
    fancyfml <- as.Formula(fml)
    formula(fancyfml, rhs = 1, lhs = 0) # ~a + b
    formula(fancyfml, rhs = 2, lhs = 0) # ~c + s

It would be a nice enhancement of `f_rhs` could also get this capability!
Cheers
Jana

title: exec() call cannot be debugged and freezes R session
description:
I am using rlang 0.4.0 and its `exec` function to call a function multiple times with variable arguments. Here's a 

``` r
library(tidyverse)

foo <- function(.df) {
  print(nrow(.df))
}

args = list(
  .df = do.call(data.frame, replicate(60000, rep(FALSE, 10000), simplify=FALSE))
)

exec(foo, !!!args)
#> [1] 10000
```

<sup>Created on 2019-07-31 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

The program completes rather quickly, despite the argument list being quite large (2.2 Gb). However, once I set a breakpoint in the `print` line, the R session hangs, the CPU is spiking at 100%, and the Rstudio debugger is not showing its tools (I subsequently have to kill Rstudio and the R session).

When I change the `exec` call to a simple `foo(args$.df)`, everything works as expected. The debugger is able to attach to the `print` line and I can use it interactively.

I've cross-posted this [here](https://github.com/rstudio/rstudio/issues/5158), but I *think* these are two issues: the first one being the `exec` code hanging (and `exec` doing something weird that causes the code to become un-debuggable), and the second one being Rstudio becoming unresponsive and not being able to kill the session.

title: easier way to create formulas using `rlang`?
description:
I am completely revamping my package codebase using the `{{` operator and so far it has been a wonderful experience. But the one domain in which I have found using `rlang` to be difficult is in creating a formula.

For example, the following code (from [SO](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/57209284/creating-a-new-formula-of-type-x-y-using-rlang/57210448#57210448)) is needed to create expression of type `~x + y`
```r
# correlation analysis
tryfn <- function(data, x, y) {
  stats::cor.test(
    formula = rlang::new_formula(NULL, rlang::expr(!!rlang::enexpr(x) + !!rlang::enexpr(y))),
    data = data,
    method = "pearson"
  )
}
```

As can be seen, this is a very complicated way to create a formula and I was wondering if there is a simpler way to do the same. This will also be helpful for me to create other kinds of formula (e.g., `y ~ x | z `).

title: Adding dispatch to `is_*()` for `quo_is_*`
description:
## Context

I was working with passing arg to a function where the default is `NULL`. The arg is `enquo()`ed, and then I need to check if the `quosure` is `NULL`. I also have another argument which is `NULL` by default, and checked. 

For reproducibility, let's imagine the function is: 

``` r 
library(rlang)
library(ggplot2)
gg_this <- function(
  df, 
  column, 
  group = NULL, 
  color = NULL
){
  
  group <- enquo(group)
  column <- enquo(column)
  if (is_null(color)){
    color <- "red"
  }
  
  if (quo_is_null(group)){
    gg <- ggplot(df, aes(!!column))
  } else {
    gg <- ggplot(df, aes(!!column, fill = !!group))
  }
  gg + geom_bar(color = color)
}

gg_this(iris, Sepal.Length)
gg_this(iris, Sepal.Length, Species)
```

## Suggestion 

I think there is a little bit of friction in not being able to use `is_null` directly on a quosure and get a TRUE/FALSE. For example one would expect: 

``` r 
x <- NULL
x <- enquo(x)
is_null(x)
```

to return TRUE, at least with `{rlang}`.

In my app I've written a little S3 dispatch: 

``` r
is_null <- function(x){
  UseMethod("is_null")
}

is_null.default <- function(x){
  rlang::is_null(x)
}

is_null.quosure <- function(x){
  rlang::quo_is_null(x)
}
```

Which could be translated in `{rlang}` directly:

``` r
is_null <- function(x){
  UseMethod("is_null")
}

is_null.default <- function(x){
  .Call(rlang_is_null, x)
}

is_null.quosure <- function(x){
  .Call(rlang_quo_is_null, quo)
}

```

Let me know if you think this is a good idea, I'll be happy to PR. 

I think this might also apply to `quo_is_call` / `quo_is_missing` / `quo_is_symbol` / `quo_is_symbolic`.

title: `with_handlers` doesn't preserve handler order
description:
For `withCallingHandlers` and `tryCatch`, conditions are checked by the applicable handlers *in the order in which they were specified*.  E.g., with the following handlers, a warning message would be be checked by both handlers: 

```r
# prints "CONDITION", then "WARNING"
withCallingHandlers(warning("woops!"),
              condition = function(x) print("CONDITION"),
              warning = function(x) {print("WARNING"); cnd_muffle(x)})
```

However, `with_handlers` only respects order *within* exiting/calling classes.  The following only checks the warning handler:

```r
# prints only "WARNING"
with_handlers(warning("woops!"),
              condition = calling(function(x) print("CONDITION")),
              warning = exiting(function(x) { print("WARNING")}))
```

Would it not make sense to change this arguably unintuitive arrangement? Letting users specify the order the handlers are checked would give them more control and make input more consistent with other base condition-handling code. It seems like the following code could do the same thing but would preserve order:

```r
with_handlers <- function(.expr, ...) {
  handlers <- list2(...)
  is_calling <- map_lgl(handlers, inherits, "rlang_box_calling_handler")
  handlers <- map_if(handlers, is_calling, unbox)
  handlers <- map(handlers, as_function)
  expr <- quote(.expr)
  
  for (i in 1:length(handlers)) {
    handler <- handlers[i]
    if (is_calling[[i]]) 
      expr <- expr(withCallingHandlers(!!expr, !!!handler))
    else
      expr <- expr(tryCatch(!!expr, !!!handler))
  }
  .Call(rlang_eval, expr, environment())
}
```

Are there any downsides to doing it this way?

title: Export vars() so dplyr, ggplot2 and purrr can reexport
`cnd_muffle`doesn't muffle conditions with different "abnormal" restarts
description:
This was mentioned in @hadley's comment in #224 : 

> I think it's reasonable to say that the signalling is always determined by the class of the condition

But see the following issue:

```r
library(rlang)
m_cond <- catch_cnd(inform("This is a message"))
with_handlers(warning(m_cond), message = calling(function(x) cnd_muffle(x)))
# Error in invokeRestart("muffleMessage") : 
#  no 'restart' 'muffleMessage' found
```

The problem is that the stock signaling functions (`stop`, `warning`, and `message`) all can take in a condition as an argument and signal that condition (without changing it), while throwing the restart methods of their "canonical" condition.

If the point of `cnd_muffle` is to muffle the conditions, shouldn't it be looking at the available restarts, rather than the class of the condition?  If you're already having to pray that restarts and condition classes have a 1-to-1 correspondence, isn't it a safer prayer that the first restart with "muffle" in its name will muffle the condition? 

The only downside I can see from doing the latter is if a user starts adding custom restarts with "muffle" in the name that **DON'T** muffle the condition. But what's more likely: that a user does something as simple as `warning(m_cond)`, or that a user is advanced enough to add custom restarts but would still rely on `cnd_muffle`?

I think the following would work just as well, but perhaps `computeRestarts` is very costly?

```r
cnd_muffle <- function (cnd) {
  possibleRestarts <- computeRestarts(cond)
  muffleRestarts <- possibleRestarts[grepl("muffle", Map(function(x) x$name, possibleRestarts))]
  resumeRestarts <- possibleRestarts[grepl("resume", Map(function(x) x$name, possibleRestarts))]
  if (length(muffleRestarts)) {
    invokeRestart(muffleRestarts[[1]])
  } else if (length(muffleRestarts)) {
    invokeRestart(resumeRestarts[[1]])
  } else {
    abort("Can't find a muffling restart")
  }
}

```

title: Include package::function information
description:
I was thinking it would make profiling/error identification a lot easier if there was an argument/option for `abort`, `warn`, etc. to include information about the package and function where the signal was raised.

This is my "manual" version of the kind of behavior I am thinking about; the `windower` function is just a dummy function used to raise an exception:
```
windower <- function(x) {
  if(!is.numeric(x)) {
    pf <- environmentName(parent.frame())
    func <- match.call()[[1]]
    pf_func <- paste0("`", pf, "::", func, "`")
    rlang::abort(paste0(pf_func, " was expecting a numeric value."))
  }
}
windower(letters)
```
This would be the error:
```
Error: `R_GlobalEnv::windower` was expecting a numeric value.
```
I'm guessing my example is a lot easier to implement because I'm in the actual environment raising the exception.

title: Space insertion when converting dashes
description:
When I do:

`rlang::quo(first-second)`

The output is:

```
<quosure>
expr: ^first - second
env:  global
```
Which inserts spaces around the dash. Is this expected behaviour? I would expect
it would return:

```
<quosure>
expr: ^first-second
env:  global
```
With no spaces.

title: Results of as_function() should inherit from "function"
description:
Functions created using `as_function()` do not have a class that includes `"function"`, which means that `inherits(fn, "function")` confusingly returns `FALSE`.

``` r
library(rlang)
# An example function, created with as_function()
is_positive <- as_function(~ . > 0)
# It is a function, as expected
is.function(is_positive)
#> [1] TRUE
# It's also a lambda, as expected 
is_lambda(is_positive)
#> [1] TRUE
# It doesn't inherit from function, which isn't expected
inherits(is_positive, "function")
#> [1] FALSE
```

A possible fix would be to change this line

https://github.com/r-lib/rlang/blob/master/R/fn.R#L436

from

```r
structure(fn, class = "rlang_lambda_function")
```

to

```r
structure(fn, class = c("rlang_lambda_function", "function"))
```

title: expr() within a tibble is messy
description:
Hi,

I've been experimenting with ways of doing selective data import of a very large CSV dataset (300-500 columns; 250,000 rows) by calculating which columns are needed for particular cohorts of data, skipping the ones which aren't needed and ergo skipping the post-import processing of those columns.

This led to me experimenting with having a tibble of the post-processing instructions - allowing the meta of being able to manipulate the instructions for building the data in much the same way as I'm manipulating the data.

Below is a table of two trivial sample rows of instructions - in this case simple conversions of a factor which is 'Y', 'N', NA to logical variables:

```
transforms_table <-
  tibble::tribble(
    ~transform_type, ~input_column, ~output_column, ~true_value, ~false_value, ~transform_function,
    "csv_factor_to_yn_logical", "S1ArriveByAmbulance", "S1ArriveByAmbulance", "Y", "N",
    rlang::exprs("S1ArriveByAmbulance" = factor_to_new_islogical_tf(
                .data[["S1ArriveByAmbulance"]], "Y", "N")
                ),
    "csv_factor_to_yn_logical", "S1OnsetInHospital", "S1OnsetInHospital", "Y", "N",
    rlang::exprs("S1OnsetInHospital" = factor_to_new_islogical_tf(
                .data[["S1OnsetInHospital"]], "Y", "N")
                )
)

```

The first problem is you can't form the expression using expr (unless you have a second column for the LHS) - otherwise you get unused argument errors).

You can however use exprs() where the LHS is treated as a named list of expressions.

I had expected at this point to do a simple splice and mutate:

```
  if (length(transforms_table[[1]] > 0)) {
    imported_data <- dplyr::mutate(imported_data,
      !!! transforms_table[["transform_function"]])
  }
```

However, because you've used exprs() in each row you're now dealing with a list of exprs() and not a column which you can treat as exprs().

You can unlist the column after creation which works.


I think the root cause of this problem is that
`list(expr("A" = my_fun(b), expr("C" = my_fun(d)) 
`

is invalid syntax, whereas:

```
my_exprs <- list(exprs("A" = my_fun(b)), exprs("C" = my_fun(d))) 
unlist(my_exprs)
```

Generates exprs without problems.

Any thoughts? Have I missed something here? Is there a better way to do this?

title: Allow `enquo` to accept string arguments?
description:
Thanks for the great package! I am just starting to understand all this, so forgive me if I missed something.

I have a function with about 50 parameters (I know that's not ideal) and I want do the same custom evaluation for them all with a function called `obj$eval_one` or `obj$eval_many`, and I am trying to avoid having 50 statements like this:

```r
param <- obj$eval_one(!! rlang::enquo(param))
```
After much pain, I managed to get it to work like this:

```r
raw_arguments <- as.list(match.call()[-1])
arguments <- obj$eval_many(!!! rlang::eval_tidy(rlang::call2(rlang::enquos, !!! rlang::syms(names(raw_arguments)))))
names(arguments) <- names(raw_arguments)
for (i in seq_along(arguments)) {
  assign(names(arguments)[i], arguments[[i]])
}
```
I originally hoped I could do this:

```r
raw_arguments <- as.list(match.call()[-1])
arguments <- obj$eval_many(!!! rlang::eval_tidy(rlang::enquos(names(raw_arguments))))
names(arguments) <- names(raw_arguments)
for (i in seq_along(arguments)) {
  assign(names(arguments)[i], arguments[[i]])
}
```
 
But `enquo`/`enquos` cannot accept strings. Would this be a useful/possible addition, or is there a better way to approach this?

Thanks!

title: Why does expr_text() behave differently for variables containing non-ASCII characters?
description:
(original issue: https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/issues/3017)

If the expression is a symbol and it has any non-ASCII characters, `expr_text()` adds backticks *except when the character is at the head of the variable name*. I'm failing to see the rule behind this... Is this intended? I feel backticks should not be added at all as long as the characters are representable in the current locale.

``` r
library(rlang)

expr_text(sym("áa"))
#> [1] "áa"
expr_text(sym("aá"))
#> [1] "`aá`"
as_string(sym("aá"))
#> [1] "aá"

aá <- 1
aá
```

title: cnd_muffle missing the 'function' class
description:
`cnd_muffle` has a class of `calling` and `handler` but does _not_ have a class of `function`. This means that functions which normally work for functions will fail on `cnd_muffle`.

https://github.com/r-lib/rlang/blob/05f778f39ac66412d78bf97c5ae01874ab0f7c4b/R/cnd.R#L555

e.g.

``` r
as.list(rlang::cnd_signal)
#> $cnd
#> 
#> 
#> $.cnd
#> 
#> 
#> $.mufflable
#> 
#> 
#> [[4]]
#> {
#>     validate_cnd_signal_args(cnd, .cnd, .mufflable)
#>     invisible(.Call(rlang_cnd_signal, cnd))
#> }
as.list(rlang::cnd_muffle)
#> Error in as.vector(x, "list"): cannot coerce type 'closure' to vector of type 'list'
```

<sup>Created on 2018-12-06 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.2.1)</sup>

I don't know if the omission is intentional, but if not it would be nice to add the `function` class.

title: Unquoting argument names with := fails in expr and quo
description:
I’ve noticed that unquoting argument names in a call via `:=` does not work inside `expr` and `quo`. Is this intentional? If so, how am I supposed to achieve the equivalent?

## MWE

```r
library(rlang)

x = sym('y')

(e = expr(list(!! x := 1)))
eval_bare(e)

(q = quo(list(!! x := 1)))
eval_tidy(q)
```

## Expected output

```
list(y = 1)
$y
[1]

<quosure>
expr: ^list(y = 1)
env:  global
$y
[1]
```

## Actual output

```
list(`:=`(y, 1))
Error: `:=` can only be used within a quasiquoted argument

<quosure>
expr: ^list(y := 1)
env:  global
Error: `:=` can only be used within a quasiquoted argument
```

Analogously with e.g. `tibble::tibble(!!x := 1)` I would expect the above to work. From what I understand of rlang from the documentation, it *should* work.

title: Difference between ensym and sym when using element of vector
description:
I'm not sure if this is desired behavior or not, but I have run into an unintuitive difference between `sym` and `ensym` when attempting to loop through a vector of strings:

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
test_df <- data_frame(g = sample(LETTERS[1:2], 30, replace=TRUE),
                      x = rnorm(30))

# using `ensym`
test_function <- function(variable){
    test_df %>% group_by(g) %>% summarise(mean(!!ensym(variable)))
}
test_function('x')           # works
test_function(letters[24])   # doesn't (surprisingly)
test_function(x)             # works

# using `sym`
test_function <- function(variable){
    test_df %>% group_by(g) %>% summarise(mean(!!sym(variable)))
}
test_function('x')           # works
test_function(letters[24])   # works
test_function(x)             # doesn't (as expected)
```

title: Branch selection in calltrace / adding a calltrace to an error
description:
For use in testthat, but could be used elsewhere as well

```r
add_calltrace <- function(code) {
  withCallingHandlers(code,
    error = function(e) {
      x <- calltrace()

      # Find second-to-last tree
      # Last tree is handleSimpleError etc
      toplevel <- which(x$parents == 0)
      n <- length(toplevel)
      start <- toplevel[n - 1]
      end <- toplevel[n] - 1

      throw(conditionMessage(e), trace = x[start:end])
    }
  )
}
```

title: Should trace_back() trim one layer of sibling calls?
description:
This would make it easier to use. Unlike `cst()` it's not meant to understand the call stack but to capture an useful backtrace. The following should all produce an empty trace:

```r
trace_back()
#> █

identity(trace_back())
#> █
#> └─identity(trace_back())

identity(identity(trace_back()))
#> █
#> ├─[ identity(...) ]
#> └─identity(trace_back())
```

title: calltrace should have strip = 1L argument
description:
To replace current line:

```
trace <- trace[-length(trace)] # remove call to self
```

Making it easier to embed inside other functions that you don't want to capture on the trace.

title: Feature Request: Allow empty quo in group_by
description:
*@jschelbert commented on Aug 28, 2018, 8:00 AM UTC:*

I have a script where the user should be able to select some columns which are used for group_by along with some other predefined columns. It should also be possible to choose no additional columns to the predefined ones. I was wondering if this could be done using `quo`, but `quo()` or `quo(NULL)` does not work.


title: API for events and hooks
description:
- task callbacks
- hooks and events
- deferred expressions (exits)

Needs to wrap 4 actions: append, prepend, replace, get.

Appending and prepending might be handled with `push_` prefixed verbs and `prepend = FALSE` argument. Replacing would be dealt with `poke_` verbs, and we'd have `peek_` verbs to retrieve the current hooks.

title: .data pronoun using the data mask environment ancestry

The idea would be to construct the data pronoun from the data mask so that it would look up for bindings navigating up the ancestry between `.top_env` and (not including) `.env`.

title: Pre-pull request: Two-sided formula to function
calltrace fails with implicit print
description:
```R
print.foo <- function(x) {
  print(rlang::calltrace())
}
foo <- structure(list(), class = "foo")
foo
#> Error: Can't create call to non-callable object 

print(foo)
#> █
#> ├─print(foo) 
#> └─print.foo(foo) 
#>   └─print(rlang::calltrace()) 
```

Because the first call contains a promise. I worked around it in `deparse_one` with

```R
fname <- expr[[1]] # force evaluation
str <- deparse(call2(fname, quote(...)), 60L)
```

But it'd be nice to know why it happens and to add a unit test.

title: Allow for duplicated arguments to `call_modify`
description:
Some useful modification patterns are currently disallowed by the arg duplication check:

```R
tc <- quote(foo(a = 1, ..., b = 2))

## move ... towards the end
call_modify(tc, ... = NULL, ... = sym(""))
#> Error: Duplicate arguments

## modification with multiple sources
call_modify(tc, !!!ll(a = 2), !!!ll(a = 3))
#> Error: Duplicate arguments
```

Judging from the code of `call_modify` the modification of named args is incremental; so there is probably little reason to disallow duplication.

title: Should quos_auto_name() use quo_name()?
description:
And should `expr_name()` deparse any kind of object?

This is about suboptimal error messages like:

```r
grouped_mean <- function(data, summary_var, ...) {
  summary_var <- enquo(summary_var)
  group_vars <- enquos(...)

  data %>%
    group_by(!!group_vars)
}

grouped_mean(mtcars, disp, cyl, am)
#> Error in mutate_impl(.data, dots) :
#>   Column `structure(list(~cyl, ~am), .Names = c("", ""), class = "quosures")` must be length 32 (the number of rows) or one, not 2
```

Caused by `quos_auto_name()` that uses `expr_text()`

```r
x <- quos(cyl, am)
quos_auto_name(quos(!!x))
#> $`structure(list(~cyl, ~am), class = "quosures", .Names = c("", \n""))`
#> <quosure>
#>   expr: ^<S3: quosures>
#>   env:  empty

expr_text(x)
#> [1] "structure(list(~cyl, ~am), class = \"quosures\", .Names = c(\"\", \n\"\"))"
```

It doesn't seem to make sense to use a multi-line deparser to give default names to expressions? Then we should use `quo_name()` / `expr_name()`. However they don't support literal objects:

```r
expr_name(x)
#> Error: `expr` must quote a symbol, scalar, or call
```

I think objects should be deparsed using the pillar sum type. Would that make sense? Then the error message above would become:

```
Column `<S3: quosures>` must be length 32 (the number of rows) or one, not 2
```

which makes more sense.

title: Documenting quosure capture behavior
description:
By design (for the reasons @lionel- gave in #73), unquoting discards the captured argument, if the unquoted expression is not a quosure, a definition or symbolic. Because this convention is not documented, it can lead to confusion and surprise (e.g., it is not strictly true that `quo()` captures the current environment, although `?quo` claims otherwise).

Is this convention obvious, or would it be worthwhile to document it?

title: unquoting in for-loops since v0.2.0?
description:
I recently started using rlang-0.2.0 and realized that unquoting in for-loops is being performed in a way that I didn't expect (and different from rlang-0.1.6). I've included a minimal example.

I can't tell if this is a feature or a bug (since it's different from rlang-0.1.6), so I thought I'd ask.
Thanks!

## Minimal Example

```
addstuff <- function(obj, label, value) {
    obj$stuff[[label]] <- enquo(value)
    obj
}

b <- b2 <- list()
for (i in 1:3) { 
    b <- addstuff(b, paste0("entry-", i), !!i) 
}
for (i in 1:3) { 
    b2 <- addstuff(b2, paste0("entry-", i * 1), !!i)
}

sapply(b$stuff, eval_tidy)
# entry-1 entry-2 entry-3
#       1       2       3

sapply(b2$stuff, eval_tidy)
# entry-1 entry-2 entry-3
#       3       3       3
```
I don't quite understand how adding the `i * 1` suddenly causes the `!!i` values to be re-evaluated at every iteration of the loop.

Also, putting the two together in a single for-loop seems to make things "fine" (or at least returns what I was seeing using rlang-0.1.6).
```
b <- b2 <- list()
for (i in 1:3) {
    b <- addstuff(b, paste0("entry-", i), !!i)
    b2 <- addstuff(b2, paste0("entry-", i * 1), !!i)
}
sapply(b$stuff, eval_tidy)
# entry-1 entry-2 entry-3
#       1       2       3

sapply(b2$stuff, eval_tidy)
# entry-1 entry-2 entry-3
#       1       2       3
```

title: Printing quosures with calls sometimes lacks required parentheses
description:
Printing quosures does not always have parentheses around the CAR of a call when it's necessary. For example, if an anonymous function expression is unquoted into the CAR slot of a call, the required parentheses are missing and produce a strange print result for the expression:

``` r
f <- quote(function(x) x + 1)
rlang::quo((!!f)(x))
#> <quosure>
#>   expr: ^function(x) x + 1(x)
#>   env:  global
```

Extracting the expression shows that it's only the printing that's incorrect:

``` r
q <- rlang::quo((!!f)(x))
rlang::quo_get_expr(q) # correct expression
#> (function(x) x + 1)(x)
```

Another example with the same issue:

``` r
g <- quote(f + g)
rlang::quo((!!g)(x))
#> <quosure>
#>   expr: ^f + g(x)
#>   env:  global
as.call(c(g, quote(x))) # expected
#> (f + g)(x)
```

I think this could be fixed by adding a check to `call_deparse()` before deparsing the CAR to see if parentheses are needed, and insert them if so.

https://github.com/r-lib/rlang/blob/2cf70c8f41513831a02878384421e417169719a8/R/deparse.R#L432-L435

I have a local branch implementing this, and could submit a PR if that sounds OK.

title: Consider renaming backtrail

> backtrail (plural backtrails): 
> 1. A small path or trail that is not used regularly.

These concepts are pretty universally called backtraces or tracebacks in computing. 

Introducing a new term is confusing, even if the tree structure makes it slightly different than a traditional backtrace. Most users aren't interested in the difference, or looking up what a backtrail is, they just want to figure out where their code failed.

title: Invalid formula when using !! on right hand side of formula
description:
I've run into an issue with unquoting a quosure on the right-hand-side of a formula. Is this known? Is there a workaround?

```
library(rlang)
x <- sample(LETTERS[1:2], 100, replace = TRUE)
y <- 1:100
xq <- quo(x)
yq <- quo(y)
wilcox.test(y ~ x) # works
eval_tidy(quo(wilcox.test(y ~ x))) # works
eval_tidy(quo(wilcox.test(!!yq ~ x))) # works
eval_tidy(quo(wilcox.test(y ~ !!xq))) # fails with error 'invalid model formula'
```

title: Inheritance problems in new_data_mask
description:
In `new_data_mask()` when the `bottom` environment is not a child of `top` the evaluation produces confusing results. It does not raise an error initially, which I think should be the behavior. The data mask can be created, but when used for evaluation it does not work correctly. It then no longer inherits from the `parent` environment specified in


``` r
library("rlang")
# You can create a data mask manually from environments.
# In this example, we will create a mask from three environments.
# There is a top environment,
top <- new_environment(list(foo = 1, bar = "abc"))
# a middle environment which is a child of top and overrides bar,
bottom <-  new_environment(list(bar = 3))

# create a mask which specifies the top and bottom environments
mask <- new_data_mask(bottom, top = top)

# now it goes to the empty environment
env_parents(mask)
#> [[1]]
#> <environment: 0x7faf07515ee0>
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> <environment: R_EmptyEnv>

# so this won't work
try(eval_tidy(quo(foo + bar), data = mask))

# however, something like this will work
eval_tidy(quo(foo + 1), data = top)
#> [1] 2
```

I think that adding a test that the `top` environment is an ancestor of the `bottom` environment in `new_data_mask()` should avoid these issue.  I didn't dig into the source code for the C++ function that `new_data_mask()` calls. I'm happy to put this in a pull request if that's how you want to handle it.

title: `are_numeric`, `all_numeric`, and friends
description:
Not sure if this should go in [`vctrs`](https://github.com/hadley/vctrs), please feel free to let me know if this should move.

It can be handy to test whether all or things are numeric, and just like there is a `rlang::are_na`, I'm wondering if there should be this for other types?

For example

``` r
are_numeric <- function(x, ...){
  any(as.logical(lapply(x, is.numeric)))
}

all_numeric <- function(x, ...){
  all(as.logical(lapply(x, is.numeric)))
}

are_numeric(iris)
#> [1] TRUE
are_numeric(letters)
#> [1] FALSE
are_numeric(1:10)
#> [1] TRUE
all_numeric(iris)
#> [1] FALSE
all_numeric(letters)
#> [1] FALSE
all_numeric(1:10)
#> [1] TRUE
```

title: Allow keeping names with squash, similar to unlist.
description:
Currently when squashing a nested list it only maintains the innermost names, discarding information which can be important and potentially causing name collision errors.

``` r
library(purrr)
library(rlang)

pets <- list(
  pet = list(
    name = "Fluffy"
  ),
  coat = list(
    colour = "blue",
    pattern = "mearle"
  ),
  eyes = list(
    colour = "blue"
  )
)

squash(pets)
```

    ## $name
    ## [1] "Fluffy"
    ## 
    ## $colour
    ## [1] "blue"
    ## 
    ## $pattern
    ## [1] "mearle"
    ## 
    ## $colour
    ## [1] "blue"

On the other hand `unlist` has the `use.names` argument which keeps names by concatenating the names of each level.

``` r
pets %>% 
  unlist %>% 
  as.list
```

    ## $pet.name
    ## [1] "Fluffy"
    ## 
    ## $coat.colour
    ## [1] "blue"
    ## 
    ## $coat.pattern
    ## [1] "mearle"
    ## 
    ## $eyes.colour
    ## [1] "blue"

It would be nice to have an equivalent option for `squash` rather than having to collect and then manually set the names after squashing, like below.

``` r
recursive_names <- function(x, parent_name = NULL) {
  if (is.list(x)) {
    if (!is.null(parent_name)) {
      x_names <- paste(parent_name, names(x), sep = "_")
    } else {
      x_names <- names(x)
    }
    
    map2(
      x,
      x_names,
      recursive_names
    ) %>% 
      reduce(c)
  } else {
    return(parent_name)
  }
}

squash_named <- function(x) {
  setNames(
    squash(x),
    recursive_names(x)
  ) 
}

pets %>% 
  squash_named()
```

    ## $pet_name
    ## [1] "Fluffy"
    ## 
    ## $coat_colour
    ## [1] "blue"
    ## 
    ## $coat_pattern
    ## [1] "mearle"
    ## 
    ## $eyes_colour
    ## [1] "blue"

description:
This would be something similar to `case_when()`, but for mapping conditions to operations -- something like a generalized switch.

As an example, the following code:

```R

  starts_with("d") ~ prod(.),
  contains("a")    ~ sum(.),
  c("mpg", "cyl")  ~ cor(.)
)
```

would evaluate to something like:

```R

+   contains("a")    ~ sum(.),
+   c("mpg", "cyl")  ~ cor(.)
+ )
[[1]]
[1] 1.218225e+91

[[2]]
[1] 336.09

[[3]]
          mpg       cyl
mpg  1.000000 -0.852162
cyl -0.852162  1.000000
```

title: Consolidate vector coercions
description:

Also we need to distinguish between implicit and explicit coercions. Currently `as_character()` etc are used for implicit coercions as well. But we'd want explicit coercion support serialisation of e.g. numeric vectors, but that should be forbidden in implicit coercions.

title: Any API for gathering the variables from an expr (or list of exprs)?
description:
Hi,

This is really an extension on a question from https://stackoverflow.com/questions/50563895/using-rlang-find-the-data-pronoun-in-a-set-of-quosures/51955427#51955427

In a nutshell I have a large (400 item) list of expressions (not quosures - I have since established they can be safely expressions). I'm using them to operate on a larger CSV file, and I want to check the variables from the expressions to do a selective import of the dataset.

The code proposal in the example works, but takes about 5 seconds to execute, mainly because of having to convert each expression in the AST into a list and then recursively act on the list. I can optimise the code somewhat but unless it is pre-executed it surprisingly will be slower than just importing the entire dataset. It also relies upon variables being identified by the .data pronoun (which I can do within the code but is not an ideal generic solution).

I wondered though whether there is a better approach to the problem - or whether Rlang itself exposes a way of gathering a list of variables from a parsed expression. Or indeed whether a function to gather a list of variables from an expression is indeed a valuable consideration for the API.

rlang:::new_lines makes illegal pairlist, not terminated by NULL
description:
rlang:::new_lines maintains a linked list, indent_status, whose elements are made with new_node(FALSE, 0L).  The second argument to new_node (eventually to Rf_cons) should be a linked list (pairlist), not 0L.  I noticed this because TERR complains about the illegal second argument to Rf_cons, but when I used R to trace the calls to new_node, with trace(rlang::new_node, quote({str(car),str(cdr)})), R crashed.  E.g.,
  > library(rlang)
  > str(new_node(FALSE, 0L))  
  
   *** caught segfault ***
  address 0x21006009, cause 'memory not mapped'

I believe the following patch will keep things legal without changing the logic of your code much.  All the testthat tests pass after the change.

```
--- /homes/bill/CRAN/rlang/R/deparse.R  2018-02-14 23:32:56.000000000 -0800
+++ ./rlang/R/deparse.R 2018-07-27 12:03:28.463628000 -0700
@@ -159,10 +159,10 @@
       status <- node_car(self$indent_status)

       if (self$next_indent_sticky) {
-        node_poke_cdr(status, inc(node_cdr(status)))
+        node_poke_cadr(status, inc(node_cadr(status)))
       } else {
         self$indent <- self$indent + 2L
-        self$indent_status <- new_node(new_node(FALSE, 0L), self$indent_status)
+        self$indent_status <- new_node(pairlist(FALSE, 0L), self$indent_status)
         self$next_indent_sticky <- TRUE
       }

@@ -176,7 +176,7 @@
       }

       reset <- node_car(status)
-      n_sticky <- node_cdr(status)
+      n_sticky <- node_cadr(status)

       # Decrease indent level only once for all the openers that were
       # on a single line
@@ -187,7 +187,7 @@
       }

       if (n_sticky >= 1L) {
-        node_poke_cdr(status, dec(n_sticky))
+        node_poke_cadr(status, dec(n_sticky))
       } else {
         self$indent_status <- node_cdr(self$indent_status)
         self$next_indent_sticky <- FALSE


```

Using purrr on quos or exprs generates plain lists
description:
If you use purrr to create expressions you get a list rather than an exprs object (and indeed if you use purrr to generate quosures you get a list, even though you've actually generated a quosures list). However I can't see a language feature which allows you to convert that list into a list of quos, so as_quosures will be FALSE (presumably unless you go and set the class attribute by hand - which sounds dangerous...)

Purrr is clearly behaving as intended - wonder whether there is scope to introduce map_quos / map_exprs objects to purrr, or whether there is benefit in an as_quosures / as_exprs in rlang which validates that all items in a list can be valid quosures / expressions and subclasses the list accordingly.

```
test <- rlang::exprs(a - b, a + b)
test2 <- purrr::map(test, ~ rlang::quo(!!.x + c))
rlang::is_quosures(test2)
rlang::is_quosure(test2[[1]])
rlang::is_quosure(test2[[2]])
```

title: env_get to evaluate a variable in the env of mutate
description:
I wanted to use env_get to evaluate a variable in the environment of the mutate call, it didn't work, while `get` did work. Example below:

Given a data frame like the following 
```
df <- tibble(n = seq(-10,10), y = rnorm(21), z = runif(21))
```
I want a function that goes inside of mutate and takes a column and uses `n`. Basically, for `y` it would be:
```
mutate(df, a = y - mean(y[n < 0]))
```
With `get`, it works:
```
baseline1 <- function(.x) {
	n <- get('n', envir = parent.frame())
	 .x - mean(.x[n < 0])
}
 mutate(df, a = baseline1(y))
```
But not with env_get:

```
baseline2 <- function(.x) {
n <-  rlang::env_get( parent.frame(), 'n')
   .x - mean(.x[n < 0])
}

mutate(df, a = baseline2(y))
```
I get a `Error in mutate_impl(.data, dots) :   Evaluation error: object 'n' not found.`

title: Document differences between base is.call and rlang::is_call
description:
Hi,

I've been using Rlang to do some code analysis. Obviously many of the RLang functions are modifications upon Base R equivalents.

Rlang::list2 for example has a number of benefits over base::list.

Checking the documentation for Rlang::is_call, I can't see why/where you would use this in preference to base::is.call (either functional benefits or speed differences). It may be that there is no benefit except for having consistent syntax - but that's not clear either!

Any thoughts on what the differences actually are?

There may be other instances of this - is_call was the example which came to mind.

title: Possible issue with scoping and `!!!`
description:
```r
library(rlang)
my_expr = exprs(FAIL=2)
eval_tidy(
  expr(transform(data, !!!my_expr)),
  env = child_env(global_env(), data = data.frame(x = 1), my_expr = exprs(SUCCESS=1))
)
#>   x FAIL
#> 1 1    2
eval_tidy(
  expr(my_expr),
  env = child_env(global_env(), data = data.frame(x = 1), my_expr = exprs(SUCCESS=1))
)
#> $SUCCESS
#> [1] 1
```

This may be my naivety, but I would have thought that the first code would add a new column named "SUCCESS" with value 1. Instead it appears that it is looking at `my_expr` from the `global_env()` instead of the environment specified in `eval_tidy()`, except only when using `!!!` (see second code).

The usage of `transform` is just a quick way to view the results of `!!!`, it was also tested with `mutate` which gave the same results.

title: cnd_type helper
inform, warn and abort could pass additional parameters on
description:
Hey - firstly, I'm really enjoying using rlang's easy condition functions.

It would be great though if the convenience functions `inform`, `warn` and `abort` could use the dots to pass on extra arguments to the `cnd_xxx` function that they call.

The reason for this is that, in the same way that these functions already use the type argument to solve the common use case "I want to raise a condition but give it some custom types", there is a second common use case of "I want to raise a condition but to include some extra information inside the condition".

Sometimes it makes sense to build a whole new function for creating those extra-information conditions, but sometimes it doesn't - and in the second case, being able to create them on the fly would be very handy.

At present you must use this sort of construct:

```
extra_info_error <- function(extra, info, variables) {
  msg <-  sprintf("some useful message", extra, info)
  rlang::cnd_error("extra_info",
    extra = extra,
    info = info,
    variables = variables,
    .msg = msg
  )
}
```
Then in your function, calling:

```
stop(extra_info_error(extra = a, info = b, variables = c)
```

With this change, you could use:
```
rlang::abort(sprintf(msg = "some useful message", a, b), type = "extra_info", extra = a, info =b, variables = c)
```
So, if you don't intend to use that sort of condition very frequently, it saves you making a function specifically for it.

title: env_parents should stop at global_env by default
description:
As env_parents is mostly useful at the REPL it should stop at `globalenv` by default. Something along these lines:


```R
#' @rdname env_parent
#' @param last Environment at which to end listing. Defaults to
#'   `global_env()`. Use `empty_env()` for the full stack that includes the
#'   search path.
#' @export
env_parents <- function(env = caller_env(), last = global_env()) {
    env <- get_env(env)
    out <- list()

    do <- TRUE
    i <- 1L 
    while (do) {
        nm <- environmentName(env)
        if (is.null(nm))
            nm <- i
        out[[nm]] <- env
        i <- i + 1L
        do <- !(is_reference(env, last) || is_empty_env(env))
        env <- env_parent(env)
    }

    out
}


```

title: Assignment function allowing arbitrary LHS?
description:
I've occasionally been annoyed that `assign` isn't as flexible as `<-`, so after some experimentation, I came up with a more general assign function that allows an arbitrary left-hand side (e.g. `assign_general(a[1], 5)` is equivalent to `a[1] <- 5`). The proof-of-concept is here: https://gist.github.com/DarwinAwardWinner/aa8b9856036a8ff93b1656fc0548697b

That script also demonstrates one of my use cases for such a feature: a function for assigning things deep into the innards of an object in the middle of a magrittr pipeline and then returning the whole object so the pipeline can continue, without resorting to something like

    `... %>% { .$a[[1]]$b[[2]] <- 3; . } %>% ...`

where the trailing dot is easy to miss when reading or writing the code. Instead, my code allows writing this as 

    `... %>% assign_into(.$a[[1]]$b[[2]] := 3) %>% ...`

I don't know how much demand or use there would be for such features, but this seems to fill a gap in R's (and rlang's) metaprogramming facilities. Is there any interest in incorporating this into rlang? If so, I can clean it up and submit it as a pull request.

title: Clean intermediate environments of the overscope
description:
As intended, `quos()` captures the calling environment:
```R
quos(x)

#> [[1]]
#> <quosure: global>
#>   ~x
#> 
#> attr(,"class")
#> [1] "quosures"
```
But if you tidyeval a quosure of `quos()`, the calling environment is not passed on to `quos()`; instead, some internally generated environment is captured (an overscope?):
```R
eval_tidy(quo(quos(x)))

#> [[1]]
#> <quosure: local>
#>   ~x
#> 
#> attr(,"class")
#> [1] "quosures"
```
I would have expected `eval_tidy(quo(quos(x)))` to capture the global environment, as `quos(x)` did (and as `eval_tidy(quo(!! quos(x)))` would).

Have I misunderstood something basic about the design/proper use of tidyeval?

title: `chr()` performance
description:
I conversation on twitter (https://twitter.com/PhilGrosjean/status/953549513054179328) mentioned that `rlang::set_names()` is much slower than `stats::setNames()`.

It turns out almost all of the performance decrease is due to the call to `chr()`

https://github.com/tidyverse/rlang/blob/c56b0aecd8efe225b11db1649c3e827674f0b662/R/attr.R#L242

If you omit the call to `chr()` when there are no dots you rescue the performance degradation almost entirely. You could do this without forcing the promise in R-devel with `...length()`, but perhaps you have a rlang function that does similar. Also you may want to think about a fast return for simple single argument vector cases of `chr()`

```diff
index 44e52035..c487af0e 100644
--- a/R/attr.R
+++ b/R/attr.R

   } else if (!is_null(nm)) {

-    nm <- chr(nm, ...)

+    }
```

title: Naming and API consistency (meta issue)
description:
rlang is still a bit unstable because one of its major goal is the consistency of its API. We think a lot about naming before introducing features but it takes some actual experience with the library to figure it out. We're aiming for reaching stability after 1 or 2 more releases. Thus rlang 0.2.0 will involve several changes, some of them backward incompatible.

This does not apply to the tidy evaluation tools exported in other tidyverse packages. These will remain completely stable. See this template for a list: https://github.com/r-lib/usethis/blob/master/inst/templates/tidy-eval.R

We are working on https://github.com/lionel-/oldie to ease up the transition, deprecated functions will still work silently for one release but it will be possible to make them noisy so that package authors can detect changes early. In particular the next version of testthat promotes all deprecation levels so packages using testthat will be alerted of changes quickly.


### Fixable with deprecation cycle

- More consistent use of abbreviations:

  Complements should not be abbreviated:

  ```r
  is_environment <- is_env
  get_environment <- get_env
  get_expression <- get_expr
  is_language <- is_lang
  ```

  Return values should be abbreviated:

  ```r
  parse_quo <- parse_quosure
  ```

  Piecewise constructors should not be abbreviated and should start with `new_` prefix:

  ```r
  new_environment <- new_env
  new_logical <- lgl_len
  new_logical_along <- lgl_along
  ```

- Use `poke` instead of `set` for stateful operations:

  ```r
  node_poke_car <- mut_node_car
  env_poke <- env_set  # Though `env_set()` was not published to CRAN yet
  ```

- `set_attrs()` should act like `attributes<-` and overwrite the whole set of attributes (this is for consistency with the new `add_` vs `set_` rules, the former should be used in order to preserve existing elements). But it also should not use an abbreviation so the new behaviour can go in `set_attributes()` and this does not break compatibility.


### Backward incompatible

- Order of `new_function()` arguments should be `body, args = list(), env = caller_env()` instead of taking non-optional arguments first. This makes it more natural to create functions of no arguments programatically (e.g. flowery iterators):

  ```r
  expr <- quote(cat("blip\n"))
  new_function(expr)
  ```

  On the other hand maybe it should be `new_closure()`? We'd talk about `fn` and `function` only when primitive functions are relevant. In this case we can make it work without breaking compatibility.

- Order of `rep_along()` arguments should be reversed so it's consistent with `seq_along()` and so it's pipe-friendly.

title: parse trees and AST's
description:
A parse tree and an AST are different things.

In this doc ( http://rlang.tidyverse.org/reference/pairlist.html ) you say that expressions are structured as parse trees, but in the upcoming version of ADV-R Hadley says they are AST's. It would be good if this doc and ADV-R agreed on terms since they are both specifically tidyverse documents. 

The Wikipedia article this doc refers to ( https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parse_tree  ) specifically says that a parse tree is **not** an AST and they are not used in computer programing. 

*Parse trees concretely[clarification needed] reflect the syntax of the input language, making them distinct from the abstract syntax trees used in computer programming*

So it is at least confusing, even is they don't know any computer science, if someone digs a bit further into the links provided after reading ADV-R and ends up reading the Wikipedia article... I know it confused me :-)

And, even though I am not a "language theorist" :-), from looking at how enquo and friends work it looks to me like R structures expressions as AST's (I don't see how it could work otherwise) not parse trees. Here is an example:

``` r
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(tidyverse))
# this arithmetic expression should evalualate
# "a * b" and "c * d" before adding them
q1 <- quo(a * b + c * d)
# and in fact it does, because it is parsing into the behavior,
# not just concrete syntax, by making + the head, i.e. the function,
# and a * b and c * d the arguments.
#
# If R were just parsing the  concrete syntax "*" would be the head
# and the tail would include "a * b + c" and "d" as arguments.
#
# in the next example 
q2 <- quo((a + b))
rlang::lang_head(q2)
#> `(`
rlang::lang_tail(q2)
#> [[1]]
#> a + b
#
# The "(" is made the function even though the wikipedia
# article specifically says that an AST would not include
# things like "(". However in R "(" is a function, not just
# syntax so it makes sense to include it in an AST
```

Note the parse tree Wikipedia article refers to ast's here https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abstract_syntax_tree

I discovered a useful code-pattern using `dplyr::case_when` inside `dplyr::mutate` that works fine in `rlang 0.1.1`, but is broken in `rlang 0.1.1.9000`:

### Expected Behaviour (CRAN, 0.1.1)

```r
library(dplyr)
#>

#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':

#>     filter, lag

tbl <- tibble(x = 1:15)

#> # A tibble: 15 x 1

f <- function(tbl, var) {

  var <- enquo(var)

  tbl %>%
    mutate(new = case_when(
      (!!var) %% 15 == 0 ~ "fizzbuzz",
      (!!var) %% 3  == 0 ~ "fizz",
      (!!var) %% 5  == 0 ~ "buzz",

f(tbl, x)
```

title: Error with enquo: the argument has already been evaluated
description:
I am trying to use `enquo` in a `summary()` generic function. I'm having some trouble reproducing this - I know this is a red flag - but perhaps there is something missing about how I understand how this function works that someone can address.

A function in a package I'm developing outputs a list such as the following list, with three elements, the first a `tibble`, and the second and third `ggplot2` plot objects:

```
> x
$df
# A tibble: 1 x 8
         action   inference percent_bias_to_change_inference
          <chr>       <chr>                            <dbl>
1 to_invalidate reject_null                           60.557
# ... with 5 more variables: replace_null_cases <dbl>,
#   unstd_beta <dbl>, beta_threshhold <dbl>,
#   omitted_variable_corr <dbl>, itcv <dbl>

$thresh_plot

$corr_plot

attr(,"class")
[1] "konfound"
```

My goal is to use the name of the object as a string; I'm trying to use a function like the following to walk people through how to print each of the three list elements, but this fails on the 1st line - with `rlang::enquo(x)`:

```
summary.konfound <- function(konfound_object){
    x_quo <- rlang::enquo(konfound_object)
    x_text <- rlang::quo_text(x_quo)

    cat("Created", length(konfound_object), "forms of output. To access type: \n")
    cat("\n")

    for (name in names(konfound_object)) {
        cat(x_text, "$", name, "\n", sep = "")
        # cat(name, "\n")
    }
}
```

When I run summary, as in `summary(x)`, the error is:

```
Error in (function (x, strict = TRUE)  : 
  the argument has already been evaluated
```

It does not seem to me that the argument is evaluated until the `length()` function on the function's 7th line. Can you help me to understand why I cannot use rlang::enquo() on the name of the object passed to `summary()`? 

There are a number of Stack Overflow questions on this topic ([here](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/46571138/enquo-error-in-function-the-argument-has-already-been-evaluated), [here](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/45636310/using-dplyrs-enquo-to), and [here](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/46309408/using-dplyr-enquo-after-calling-argument)), but their answers were either inconclusive or did not seem pertinent in this case.

title: Fix parse tree for !!
description:
* Remove one layer of parentheses surrounding bang-bang, e.g. `(!! x)`. This way:

```r
x <- quote(fn)
expr(
  (!! x)(foo)
)

# expands to:
fn(foo)

# instead of:
(fn)(foo)
```

* What operator precedence do we want for `!!`? On master it's now binding very tightly, but maybe we should make some exceptions. Maybe operators that are written without space should bing tightlier than `!!`:

```r
expr(!! x:y)
```

Currently on master this is equivalent to:

```r
expr((!! x):y)
```

But maybe this should be:

```r
expr(!! (x:y))
```

There is a similar issue for `^`:

```r
expr(!! x^y)
```

title: Unquote-splicing a pairlist may mutate it
description:
Under 0.1.2.9000 and R 3.4.2, unquote-splicing a pairlist in `quo()` can mutate the pairlist itself.

Example where there should be no side-effects:
```R
x <- pairlist(0)

quo(foo(UQS(x), y))
#> <quosure: global>
#> ~foo(0, y)

x
#> [[1]]
#> [1] 0
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> y
```
The same occurs for `expr()`. `x` is not mutated if it is a list.

(Is the culprit the C function `rlang_interp()`?)

title: Should quosures be evaluated with base::eval()
description:
This would allow the call stack to be traced back.

Currently we can't because the overscope environment is not on the stack. So `sys.parents()` uses the fallback behaviour and pretends that the caller frame of the quosure is itself. Using base eval would fix this because it would create a call frame with the overscope as environment.

```r
ctxtstack <- function() ctxt_stack()

# The quosure caller is itself
eval_tidy(quo(ctxtstack()))
```
